utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Good morning. Please call the case.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good morning. Case number IT-95-9-T, the Prosecutor versus Blagoje Simic, Miroslav Tadic and Simo Zaric.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes, the Prosecution is cross-examining. MR. DI FAZIO: If Your Honours please, earlier in the week you asked me to indicate whether or not the Prosecution wished to cross-examine the expert witness, Dr. Svetlana Radovanovic, the demographics expert called by the Defence. I've had an opportunity of going through the report and I indicate that the Prosecution most certainly does wish to cross-examine that expert.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Very well. The Trial Chamber had already indicated on the date she is expected to come, that is the 26th of May. So the Prosecution will have the opportunity to cross-examine then. We will continue with cross examination of Mr. Simo Zaric.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Cross-examined by Mr. Re: [Continued]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. Zaric.

utterances.speaker: SIMO ZARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Good morning.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yesterday afternoon, Mr. Pantelic asked you some questions about Milan Simic and Stevan Todorovic. The question was, "And Stevan Todorovic had behind him his policemen and certain other personalities of dubious character." To which you answered, "yes, I agree with you." And then he asked you about a link between capital and armed force, that is, namely, "Could you tell us if you know whether any criminal activities of these two, that's Milan Simic and Stevan Todorovic, regarding smuggling of oil, et cetera, cigarettes and whiskey during the war," and that was just before the break, and your answer was, "Yes, I have information and I agree with your assessment and I can give you more information, some things that I know about, if you assess that this is relevant to speak about." We went to the break then and we didn't really return to that topic. Can you elaborate now on that information about smuggling by Mr. Todorovic and Mr. Milan Simic or others connected with them, please?

utterances.speaker: SIMO ZARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. The first and the ugliest pictures after the hostilities broke out in Bosanski Samac and what I was able to see with my own eyes, these pictures were linked to mass transfer of goods in lorries, in trailers, that came to -- in front of the public security station. There they were given the supporting transfer documents by Mr. Todorovic.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Just stop you there. Can you please tell us, I don't want you to stop you telling us but can you just tell us when this was?

utterances.speaker: SIMO ZARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This started to happen already from the 19th, 20th, 21st, immediately in the first few days after the hostilities broke out. The first few days after the conflict broke out, the first couple of days after the hostilities broke out in town. These lorries that were loaded with goods, they first of all looted the department store, from where they took out the best carpets, furniture and any other goods that were there. And then all that was transported by lorries to Serbia. Some of the information I heard later on from Mr. Savic and from Mr. Sarkanovic that they also had seen this on several occasions and I have at least seen it on two or three occasions, these lorries, they would stop, they wouldn't linger, then they would go in the direction of Serbia. I also had the information that until coordinators were established in companies in Samac, goods were transported in a similar way from factories, like for instance furniture from the Buducnost factory in Samac, then certain hot water boilers from the Mebos factory, then some of the furniture from the Uzarija factory. So this operation of mass transport of furniture was cut off at the moment when the Crisis Staff appointed coordinators who were able, to a greater or lesser extent, to prevent this. I cannot say for sure what kind of supporting transfer documents were needed for this transport when it went in an uncontrolled way to Serbia in these first few days but it is undeniable that this picture was there plain to see in the first few days of the war, until certain things came to be under some kind of control, more or less. Second thing is that what was really astonishing to me is that after a few days, possibly maximum ten to 15 days after the conflict broke out, I was informed by Mr. Cancarevic, Mr. Milos Savic and some people who worked in the public security station that in a special transport, all of the weapons that were collected in the first few days during the operation of disarming of non-Serb population and part of the Serb population who had acquired their weapons illegally, all of these weapons went to Serbia overnight, and we never heard anything about what happened to these weapons until late autumn when criminal proceedings were initiated before the military tribunal in Banja Luka and then, very timidly, there was some discussion about it, but as far as I know, there were hundreds and hundreds of pieces of all kinds of weapons, from military rifles, automatic rifles, semi-automatic rifles, pistols, from legally and illegal hunting weapons, all of this went, all this was transported to an unknown destination, rather it was -- the destination was Serbia.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Zaric, could we take this in two parts? Firstly, the department stores and so on, and secondly, the looting, sorry, weapons. So if I could just take you back to the first part and we'll come to the weapons in a moment. I don't want to stop you, please understand that. I just want to proceed in a more sequential manner. We started off, I started off by asking you about the connection between Mr. Todorovic and Mr. Milan Simic and you said you saw with your own eyes some trucks outside the SUP. What did you see -- I withdraw that. Did you see Mr. Milan Simic or Mr. Stevan Todorovic do anything in relation to those trucks, and if so, what was it?

utterances.speaker: SIMO ZARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Stevan Todorovic, I saw him personally in front of the public security station, when he was greeting these drivers who were driving the lorries in the beginning of the war, and I heard that for certain type of goods, I heard that, these are my operative information, this is my intelligence, I didn't see that, and I thought that this would be an interesting subject for certain services who -- that should have been taking care of the criminal actions, apparently I heard that apart from the supporting documents, these transfer documents, Mr. Milan Simic issued certain documents in relation to some goods as if this was legitimate transport of goods, but in fact, these goods according to my deep conviction, this -- these goods, they did not go to this warehouse in Pazova where later on it will be legally and legitimately -- goods will be transported or kept for security reasons but precisely this -- these goods went through this criminal route.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You mentioned Mr. Todorovic and Mr. Milan Simic. What about other members -- sorry, other people associated with the Crisis Staff or the Executive Board? What was your information, if any, in relation to their connection with what you saw?

utterances.speaker: SIMO ZARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: To be honest, I know that Mr. Milan Simic, during these first days of the war, was in the vicinity or he was close to the people from the Crisis Staff but whether -- whether anyone in the Crisis Staff had asked this question regarding the criminal activity and had given him authorisation to do this, I really cannot make this claim. But I do know that this was in relation to him and Mr. Todorovic initially, but I cannot claim that the Crisis Staff or someone else, some other people from the Crisis Staff, that they were standing by this criminal activity.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You also spoke about the collection of weapons and their transportation to Serbia. What was your information about who was responsible for transporting them to Serbia? And also where they went?

utterances.speaker: SIMO ZARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as I was able to find out through my intelligence, the special load of these weapons went through Bijeljina and Zvornik to the border crossing of Sepek. I think that is the name. But what happened to these weapons, I don't know. I know that the -- as far as I've heard, that these lorries were escorted by the regular police of the public security station so that reportedly these goods could pass more easily and one of the specials also went, those specials that had come from Serbia. As far as other intelligence is concerned, that this weapons were smuggled for the area of Kosovo.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In case I've missed this, can you just -- you've already said and I apologise, but can you just tell us when that was?

utterances.speaker: SIMO ZARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This could have happened by the end of April, 1992.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When you spoke to the Prosecutor or the Office of the Prosecutor on the 2nd of April, 1998, and that's your interview, that's Exhibit P140, P140 ter at page 94 to 95, I'm sorry, I said P140 in error, I meant P141, you were asked about looting in the Odzak area and your -- the Prosecutor said to you, "So this is the Samac Crisis Staff who was allowing this looting to go on," to which you answered, "Yes, many things were taken away, it was all organised by them. Many things were also hidden from me and I don't know where things were taken but I know that many things were taken then. And since then, the municipality of Vukosav Ilija has been formed, now Serbs live, and the SDS ruled. And there has been a strong polarisation conflict between them now, precisely because of all this property that Crisis Staff had smuggled away somewhere. That is the truth." The next question was, "Do you know if Blagoje Simic and Stevan Todorovic personally benefited from any of this looting?" To which you responded, "I cannot say for sure but compared to me, they have a much better life-style. They could not possibly have made that kind of money during this war." Now, your response to the Prosecutor was that it was the Crisis Staff who allowed the looting to continue and it was organised by them. What I want you to tell us now is what are the things that the Crisis Staff allowed to be taken away in this organised looting that you told the Prosecutor about in June -- sorry, April, 1998. Just before you answer, I just want to remind you of something else, that was in the third interview, which was on the 3rd of June, which is P142 ter and the question was, page 65, I'm sorry, I'm referring to P142, not P142 ter. The question was, "Well, the witnesses that we have say that you were giving out the looting assignments to people to go and steal things from whom in Odzak." You answered, "I have to laugh. It's a lie. You have a man before you, if you can only believe him a little, that I know that Odzak was looted and the Crisis Staff is behind that. Try to get these people here so... And you can only have a witness in me that would state this and talk about the fact that this happened." The next question was from the Prosecutor, "Well what do you know about the looting that occurred in Odzak?"

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: I apologise, I cannot find this in document P142, on page 65. Do we have the same document? I believe that the Trial Chamber neither can find it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Which version is this? Is it the version which also has the B/C/S at the same time or is it the other version?

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: I'm reading only from the English version which is P142, not P142 ter, that's the English-only version. Does that assist?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: No, because our page 65 doesn't have the paragraph you're talking about.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Mr. Weiner will find it in the ter version.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Let's agree from now on which version so that we all are on the same page.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Your Honours, if I remember correctly, and I believe I have here 142 ter in front of me, this is the only one that has both B/C/S and English.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: And I would like if we can arrange this with the Prosecution to refer always to these documents in order to show this to Mr. Zaric and in order to help us follow the document.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Of course. I apologise, I actually thought I was. But it was a mistake I made. I can certainly come back to finding the ter version fairly soon but I think, Mr. Zaric, you understand the question I've asked you or do you want me to find it before we go on?

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: I believe it is not a problem whether Mr. Zaric understands the question. The question was not actually posed yet. It was just a quotation but just to -- one suggestion. Maybe those P140, 141 and 142 ter should be in front of Mr. Zaric when you are already referring to this. This would simplify all this.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Of course, I have no objection to Mr. Zaric having his statements in front of him as we go.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes, and that can be put in front of the --

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: All three of them. For the Trial Chamber's and my learned friend's benefit, it's at page 137 and 138 of P142 ter. That's the B/C/S and English version.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: So we're dealing with 1-- P142 ter first. And then page 137 and 138.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Of P142 ter, that's right.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Zaric, do you need to refer to them before you -- Mr. Zaric --

utterances.speaker: SIMO ZARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't have to read the text. I've understood more or less your question.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you. My question after reading that to you is: You referred to looting organised by the Crisis Staff in Odzak. What I want you to tell the Trial Chamber based upon your answers to the Prosecutor in 1998, what was the looting and how was it organised by the Crisis Staff?

utterances.speaker: SIMO ZARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I, in the examination-in-chief, when I was examined by Mr. Pisarevic, and yesterday, I told the Trial Chamber how at this moment I am thinking in respect of these matters. This does not mean that I am trying to find a different context for the looting which, according to my mind, it was plain to see, but when I was giving this interview in 1998, and I have to say without saying it, without sufficient experience, I was not thinking about individual responsibility, and addressing certain occurrences and certain events regarding certain persons the way I see it now. That is why in the examination-in-chief I said that there was organised looting, that accomplices were also people from the command in that looting and that it was the executive board of the Municipal Assembly of Samac that was linked to that, where, in certain way, the associate for this was the President of the civilian-military council in Odzak, Mr. Savo Popovic, who, according to the nature of his work, mostly cooperated with Mr. Milan Simic as the president of the executive board and this is the reason why I wanted to stress this. However, as regards the looting itself and the way I saw that, I can state that not a single lorry of goods could have gotten out of the municipality of Odzak without the accord for taking any kind of goods being given by the military command. This did not mean that the goods couldn't be transported to Bosanski Samac, that the goods could not have been transported in direction of Banja Luka from where mostly these Krajina units had come, that they couldn't have come -- they couldn't have gone individually according to the requests of commands of the -- depending on the request of certain people from the military command, so from the way I saw it, some of the goods must have legitimately gone for the needs of the army and the people, but the other part of the goods, and this is my deep conviction, went regardless of those signatures, that were there, and people -- regardless of the people who followed the transport of the goods, and these goods did have a criminal route, even this was signed -- even if this was signed by the president of military administration and even if it was signed by Mr. Popovic, the president of the military and civilian council.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Zaric, when you spoke to the Prosecutor, your -- you did so in the presence of your lawyer, Mr. Pisarevic, on both occasions in April and June, 1998, and we can assume that he gave you some extensive advice about the sorts of things that you would be asked, based upon what was in the indictment, and the sorts of questions you would give, can't we?

utterances.speaker: SIMO ZARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: To be quite honest, my counsel gave me full freedom to answer the Prosecutor's questions and, for example, we did not discuss this topic, nor did I think it was necessary to do so. When I said Crisis Staff at that point in time, I was starting from the fact that Mirko Jovanovic was the first president of the executive board of the municipal assembly and he was an ex officio member of the Crisis Staff, at least that's what he said. When he was replaced by Milan Simic as the president of the executive board of the municipal assembly, I thought then that automatically, Mr. Milan Simic was a member of the body called the Crisis Staff, which was the narrowest body. Savo Popovic, who, ex officio, was the president of the civilian-military council, was a member of the Crisis Staff, and when I mentioned the word "Crisis Staff" I thought that these people who in my view were directly connected to the departure of some of the goods which I felt were being taken away in a criminal way, were people connected to the Crisis Staff. That was the reason I attributed this to the Crisis Staff, and to be quite honest, to this day I still fail to understand the real way in which responsibility was divided between the executive board and the Crisis Staff during the war.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. Remember yesterday you said you would try and listen to the question and answer the one which I asked? The question I asked you was about your speaking to your lawyer and advice. It wasn't about the other things. I want to ask you separately about those things. Would you be able to please concentrate on the question?

utterances.speaker: SIMO ZARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Very well. I just felt it necessary to explain to the Trial Chamber why I said what I did. I am not trying to avoid this topic, not at all.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Look, I'm not suggesting you are. There are some questions I want to ask you. You can answer them and of course Mr. Lazarevic -- sorry, Mr. Pisarevic will clear up anything that he thinks I've left uncovered or requires explanation. Look, when Mr. -- sorry, when the Prosecutor interviewed you, they asked you some fairly specific questions about looting and both in April and in June, 1998, you knew, didn't you, who the members of the Crisis Staff had been in 1992 and the War Presidency, thereafter, 1992 and 1993?

utterances.speaker: SIMO ZARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I had my opinion as to who exactly were the members of the Crisis Staff and who were the members of the War Presidency, but I never saw any decisions appointing any one of them. However, because of the way they behaved, because of the positions they held, because they often associated at various meetings, that was the conclusion I drew.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Your answers were very specific to the Prosecutor. It's at page 94 of the interview of April, 1998. The question, "so this is the Samac Crisis Staff who was allowing this looting to go on?" Your answer was, "yes, many things were taken away."

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: What is the evidence number?

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: P141, 141 ter, at page 94.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: That's the second interview on the 2nd of April.

utterances.speaker: SIMO ZARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have found page 94.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The first question from the top in italics, "so this is the Samac Crisis Staff who is allowing this looting to go on?" To which your answer, in the italics, is, "Yes, many things were taken away." Do you see that there? I'm just asking if you see it first.

utterances.speaker: SIMO ZARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: If -- no, I don't see exactly what you said, because here the sentence begins as follows, "Yes, it was organised by them. Where it was all taken off to be quite sincere, many things are concealed from me. Are you -- is this the part of the text you want me to look at?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes, the question preceding where it's gotten written, Nancy, meaning Nancy Paterson, "so this is the Samac Crisis Staff who was allowing this looting to go on?" To which your answer was, "Yes, many things were taken away?"

utterances.speaker: SIMO ZARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes, I found the text.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: If you just read down to the next question, again Nancy, "Do you know if Blagoje Simic and Stevan Todorovic personally benefited from any of this looting?" And your answer was, "I cannot say for sure but compared to me, they have a much letter life-style. They could not possibly have made that kind of money during the war" -- I'm sorry, "during this war." And your answer is on the bottom of the page. You see that there, don't you?

utterances.speaker: SIMO ZARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes. I see this.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What I'm just saying to you or asking you is that when asked you gave a very specific answer nominating the Crisis Staff as being responsible for it. You said they were -- you said it was all organised by them and then, when the Prosecutor asked you about Mr. -- Dr. Simic and Mr. Todorovic, your answer was, "I cannot say for sure," but you didn't nominate anyone else but what you said was they have a much better life-style which you would accept indicates that you're implying that they benefited in a way that you didn't from looting?

utterances.speaker: SIMO ZARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Such a conclusion might be drawn. The Prosecutor did not ask me about other people and I wasn't answering questions that were not put to me at the time, and I replied that I was not asserting this, but that Mr. Blagoje Simic and Stevan Todorovic had a better life-style than I did, I said that because I was asked directly about these two and no one else. That's why I said what I did. I have to admit that these are people who before the war and during the war and probably even today are better off than I was, and they were better off at the time.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, the Prosecutor asked you about organised -- about looting in Samac, you replied that it was organised by the Crisis Staff. You knew who the Crisis Staff members were or the War Presidency members were, you didn't nominate any, like Mr. Popovic or Mr. Milan Simic. All you said was that it was the Crisis Staff or you agreed that it was the Crisis Staff who had organised it.

utterances.speaker: SIMO ZARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, if the entire body is to be personified in one person, that's the impression one can get. At the time I was not in my mind separating Milan Simic or Stevan Todorovic or Savo Popovic from the Crisis Staff. That is why, when giving an overall estimate, I mentioned the body in which these people worked and in my view through them or with their cooperation, certain criminal actions were being taken, were taking place, which I saw, and that's why I gave the answer I did and I have not changed my standpoint in this respect.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Zaric, you have written a book, and you've been interviewed by the media in relation to what happened, and you gave seven days of testimony in examination-in-chief, and you worked for the intelligence service.

utterances.speaker: SIMO ZARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Excuse me, I am not hearing the interpretation.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Your Honour --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Can we have something done?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, I can hear now but a short while ago, I didn't hear anything when Mr. Re started asking his question.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Zaric --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Is it all right with everybody now?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] A short while, Mr. Tadic was trying to signal to me that he couldn't hear. Perhaps someone from the technical booth could check his headset.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Can we have that tested? Can you hear now, Mr. Tadic? Yes, can you hear now? A technician is coming. It's all right now? Yes, we can proceed.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Zaric --

utterances.speaker: SIMO ZARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You worked for intelligence service for many years, you've written a book, you've been interviewed by the media about what happened in Bosanski Samac, and you testified in examination-in-chief for seven days. Did you make notes at the time, when all these events occurred, from which you referred to write your book, give your interviews, make your statement to the Prosecutor and give your seven days of very detailed testimony about the events?

utterances.speaker: SIMO ZARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I am, by nature, a person who always kept notes. However, during my testimony, I was not in a position to make notes. I'm referring to these past seven days. However, previously, I often wrote notes which I used when making assessments, and writing parts of the book I wrote while in detention here.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Part of your work in intelligence of course involved making notes and keeping records and keeping very careful records, didn't it?

utterances.speaker: SIMO ZARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. But I have to say that it was not the practice for an operative to take original notes home. This was not done in the former Yugoslavia or anywhere else in the world. However, I did have some material at home which I was able to use to refresh my memory of certain events. An operative or a member of an intelligence service cannot keep confidential archives at his home.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you keep a diary during the war? 1991, 1992, 1993.

utterances.speaker: SIMO ZARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: One might call it a diary. I did write quite a lot, and I have a lot of material which might be termed a war diary or war notes and which I used when arriving at certain standpoints.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was it a diary that you wrote in every day to record things that had happened, important events?

utterances.speaker: SIMO ZARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As a rule, I tried to note the most important events of the day, or the past few days, if things were not happening on a daily basis.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And is it -- what sort of record is it? A notebook or an exercise book? What did you keep -- what did you record these important events of the day in?

utterances.speaker: SIMO ZARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I had work books sometimes. Sometimes small pads. And depending on the topic. For example, I had a special notebook where I kept notes on everything that happened at the command. If I was visiting certain units, I had a special pad in which I wrote down what I heard and what I talked about with people in the units I visited. If there were other topics to write about, I had small notepads. So that there were different notebooks, there was more than one, depending on the topic I was dealing with at any given moment. I also had a special notepad for notes on interviews with people who had been refugees and who were talking about things that had happened to them. So there were a lot of notes in various notepads which I kept at home and where I tried to enter the most important information from these interviews, meetings and so on. This was the method I used, more or less.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What were the topic --

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: I apologise. There is something unclear here in the record. I don't believe that Mr. Zaric said that he kept these pads at home and here it says on page 17, line 14, because previously he said you don't usually take these kind of notes at home.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: I'll ask him to clarify it, then.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: No. What he said about note -- what he was not allowed to keep at home was the work, the notes of an intelligence officer, I think. Any way, you can ask him to clarify it.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Zaric, the notepads that we heard interpreted as you taking or keeping at home, were they the ones you just referred to, not your official ones but private ones in which you recorded important events, meetings, people you'd spoken to and what was happening?

utterances.speaker: SIMO ZARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Precisely so. But if I was drawing up an official document on the basis of these notes, I'm talking now about the pre-war situation, when I was a member of the state security service, and if this was put into an official statement or an official note on intelligence information I had gathered, then I could not keep that document in my own archives but had to submit it to the competent organ in Doboj where my superior was, and to whom I was responsible. But I kept the working material with me.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: "I kept the working material with me." Can you just tell us what that means? Which working material are you referring to? And whether you mean at home?

utterances.speaker: SIMO ZARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I am speaking of the working material I kept during the war when I was assistant commander, both of the 4th Detachment and later on when I went to the brigade or when I took notes of what happened at the meeting, for example, of the 17th of August, when I visited a unit, and spoke of the reasons for the drop in morale, then I would take notes on this and then I would use these notes to draw up an official document informing the official command. The document was a summary. It was -- it contained the most important information, but my notes were more extensive and they contained details that were not necessary, that need not be included in the document.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did that include assessments of people and their reactions to things or their motives, the sort of things intelligence officers are trained to put in background information or look for?

utterances.speaker: SIMO ZARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: When I became assistant commander for morale, I was no longer an intelligence officer. I was a morale officer. When I was in the 4th Detachment, then I was assistant commander for intelligence and security and then, when I drew up written information, whether it was an official note or whether it was a statement, I submitted that to Mr. Makso Simeunovic.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What I was asking you was about the personal notes you kept which you didn't submit and I'm asking that based upon your training in intelligence, where you gather information about people and you might write up something or make notes about your impressions or reactions or what you thought a person's motives were. All I'm asking you is these notes you made during the war, I'm sorry, between 1991, 1992 and 1993 the notes that you made and kept at home and didn't submit, did they also include things such as that, assessments of people's motives and why they were saying things? Or your own conclusions?

utterances.speaker: SIMO ZARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In these work books and notebooks, I wrote down the conversations as they took place, but my assessments, I included in the official documents which I submitted. There is a difference here. If I was talking to someone and they told me, for example, that there had been criminal actions or that the soldiers were not satisfied with the food or that the officers were not fulfilling their tasks, I didn't say to the -- I didn't then, in the work book, give descriptions of whether I thought the officer was acting properly or not. I didn't enter that in my work books.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. Well, what were the subject topics of each of these notebooks, if you could just list them for us?

utterances.speaker: SIMO ZARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's impossible. That's hundreds of topics, hundreds of topics. I really cannot answer in this direction, but if I was speaking in a unit or there were topics, what kind of food it was, whether the troops were going to the front lines, to the positions, were there deserters, what kind of problems did they have in the local communes, how did they see these problems, what was the relationships to the families of those who can be killed or injured, some had been asking questions regarding the problems, is there a chance for shifts to be longer, so that they could sow the wheat, there were hundreds of topics, Mr. Prosecutor, it was war. I couldn't possibly give you a satisfactory answer to this question and I can't possibly tell you that my memory is this strong for me to recall every single topic that I dealt with in my work book.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Is what you're saying that each thing had a -- or each area or subject had its own separate notebook? And you kept hundreds of notebooks?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Re, why are we going into this area of how the accused was working, taking notes, keeping -- what's the purpose of this?

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: I can certainly make it relevant, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes, what is it?

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Well, can I ask him?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: No, no. I want to find out from you.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Well, I want to know where the notebooks are. I want to know whether he referred to them in giving his evidence here, in writing his book, in making his statement.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: You want to know whether he had his notebooks and he was referring to them during the interviews?

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: No but if I could ask the question, I could probably get the answer. I'm sure Mr. Zaric will inform us of whether he did refer to them.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: I hope we won't take too long on this.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: We won't, Your Honour, if he answers it.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You understand, Mr. Zaric, what I want to know is did you refer to those notebooks -- I withdraw that. The notebooks, of course, had dates in them, didn't it, dates of events?

utterances.speaker: SIMO ZARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In most cases, yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Those notebooks, you recorded conversations with people such as Lieutenant Colonel Nikolic? And Dr. Simic? Of important events?

utterances.speaker: SIMO ZARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In those work notes, work books, there were also such notes, if I had had any such conversations, then I would write down what I heard in -- during a conversation. That's true.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Including the arrival of the paramilitaries, the Crkvina massacre, murders in police custody, in the SUP? Those are the sort of details you recorded in the notebooks?

utterances.speaker: SIMO ZARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Many things, Mr. Re. This person sitting here knows many things, even if there were no work books.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I'm just asking --

utterances.speaker: SIMO ZARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: But I'll allow that some of the assessments --

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I'm just asking you whether you recorded the arrival of the paramilitaries, the Crkvina massacre and murders in police custody in the SUP in these notebooks you kept.

utterances.speaker: SIMO ZARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Presume that in a work book of mine, if I was going to meetings of the local staff Crisis Staff at the local commune of Samac, it is certain that I would write somewhere or that somebody would ask me, some of the people, since one of the topics must have been the arrival of those specials and probably something must have been written in those work books on this subject, that is not to be denied. But later on, I investigated this problem thoroughly and when I was working on this information, and when I had the opportunity to have something behind me, that is when I came to relatively respected position at the command of the brigade, then that was not a problem for me to, while collecting the information, I would get to the relevant dates and the relevant events that were written in the information.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Zaric, when you wrote your book, you referred to these extensive notebooks, didn't you? And you used them as the basis for many of the things you wrote in your book, events, conversations, dates, times, places?

utterances.speaker: SIMO ZARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In one part, I'd agree, and in one part, what I was interested in and what perhaps I wasn't sufficiently certain of, my investigator had investigated because I kept a correspondence with him and to be honest, I was a little worried about this work book of mine because I knew that our cells are checked from time to time so I thought that somebody would find it, find this, and take away or bring into question these work books, and these working material of mine, so when I received certain information, then I would, but I have to tell the Trial Chamber how it came that I had enough strength to write a book. Ten or 15 days, as far as I can remember, I would write certain notes down, the main topics, and then I would send that to my investigator in Belgrade, and then this was -- this went to my associates who promised me that this book was -- would be published and my only wish regarding this book is so that I wanted to express that my pre-war and my war biography would be recorded and that everything I'd lived through in the war I would point to the heavy part of the truth that happened, which does not mean that at some point these associates who helped me regarding the language and who also helped me with the stylistic refinement of certain sentences because they noticed that I was perhaps nervous and that I had trouble with formulating certain sentences and there were certain things that I did not agree with, but later on, when the book was published, it was too late for any kind of intervention from me to make and I just have to tell the Trial Chamber that I'm the kind of person who only speaking Ijekavica that is, Bosnian mother tongue when there is no Ekavica dialect and this is not a dialect which is used in Bosnia, but as it happened, my book was published as if I was living in Belgrade. It was published in Ekavica and I was so angry because of that, because this was done. The preface to this book which was written by a member of the academy, Professor Nedeljkovic, it does not correspond to what I am as a man, but I had no influence because these associates of mine who helped me publish this book, they did not take into consideration everything that tomorrow or the day after tomorrow would be relevant for this Tribunal, and I believe that this book cannot be considered, that it had been written regarding the laws of the Tribunal, but I was trying to try out my ability to write something. There is a lot of literal things, a lot of literary things, a lot of things that are -- have some certain predispositions and certain suppositions, so I am not running away from everything in this book which is in this book, it is a mirror, it is my frame, I'm not ashamed of it but there are certain omissions of a technical nature of any other nature, and Mr. Re -- Mr. Re, if you wish to use this book to disqualify me and question my credibility, I have nothing against that, but then I would like to -- you to refer to each portion of the book so that you can question me on it.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: My question was a few minutes ago, did you refer to your notebooks when you wrote your book? Did you use them as reference material for times, dates, places, conversations? Please answer that one.

utterances.speaker: SIMO ZARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I used my memory to the best of my recollection, and some of the material that I had on me, because this information regarding the 13 signatories that has been disclosed and I had that with me, and this single information I could have written five books, not just one book.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, did you refer to those -- did you refer to your notebooks, the notes you made at the time, before giving your testimony over those seven days?

utterances.speaker: SIMO ZARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I used everything that's gone through this case so far. No Prosecution witnesses has gone without me speaking with my Defence lawyers and discussing, analysing the testimony of all the witnesses and Defence witnesses, and all the other witnesses. Mr. Re, I am very conscientious regarding this. I don't want to be arrogant and without any false modesty but I am working very hard on this and I have had a lot in front of me, and there was not a problem for me to remember what happened in Crkvina, how looting went on, what happened with Mico Djurdjevic, I lived with these problems throughout the time here, throughout the unfortunate war and to date. Everything that stayed in my head, in my mind, I cannot get rid of it.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I really don't want to interrupt you but I want to you focus us on the question. The question was simply this: Did you refer to these notebooks, the extensive notebooks you made at the time, before or during your testimony over those seven days? Did you use them to refresh your memory?

utterances.speaker: SIMO ZARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Why would I need to consult -- no, if I needed to consult, then I would give the task to my investigator to find out whether there was something in my work books, but these records, these work books, they were not with me in The Hague, in the cell, here with me, in the cell where I was, where I am.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do we take it from that that you did ask your investigator to consult these books in relation to some details before you gave your testimony? It's just a little bit unclear. I just want to know whether you referred to them either through -- you said you had not got them with you but did you get someone else to look at them to ascertain various details?

utterances.speaker: SIMO ZARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Can you specifically ask me as to what you mean? Which detail and why would I need to ask my investigator?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Your answer a moment ago was unclear. You said if I needed to consult then I would give the task to my investigator to find out whether there was something in my work books. Now I couldn't possibly know what is in your mind or what you needed to ask your investigator to consult in your work books. What I'm asking you is, did you ask your investigator to consult those notebooks or work books -- what did you call them, work books, to assist you in refreshing your memory on any aspect of your testimony?

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: I apologise. Maybe there is one misunderstanding here, I believe, right at this point. Are you referring now to these seven days, as it was mentioned previously, or during the writing of Mr. Zaric's book? What are we talking about referring to those notes and asking investigator to check out some datas, whether it was during his book was written or in last seven days, because frankly I'm a bit confused at this point.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: No. If you read the last sentence, he's talking about in any aspect of your testimony. So he's talking about the evidence that Mr. Zaric has given in the Trial Chamber.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Zaric, you heard the question, my question.

utterances.speaker: SIMO ZARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, is that -- what's the answer? Did you get your investigator to consult those work books to assist you in giving your testimony here?

utterances.speaker: SIMO ZARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I repeated this sentence so many times, I don't know why you're insisting I should repeat it again. What I wasn't certain about, when I needed it, my investigator gave me the relevant data.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Where are these work books?

utterances.speaker: SIMO ZARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: They were returned to my investigator.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: They were returned to your investigator? Who had them to return them to your investigator? Are you saying that the investigator gave them to you, you looked at them and then sent them back to your investigator?

utterances.speaker: SIMO ZARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Part of those conversations, my investigators were here on a couple of occasions, people I've spoken with, and this is uncontested.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreter didn't catch the name uttered by Mr. Zaric.

utterances.speaker: SIMO ZARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: They came here, they spoke to me, I spoke to them. And I also agreed with them the concept of the book, and through my associates, that I asked to do this, and I have to admit that my lawyers, neither Mr. Pisarevic, nor Mr. Lazarevic, were not willing for me to do this. I'm not saying that I was stubborn really in writing this book. I had the best of intentions, but if you, as Prosecutors couldn't find any use for it, then I don't know.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I'm sorry, but this is terribly unclear to me. Are you saying that the work that the investigators, your investigator brought the work books to The Hague took them to you in the detention centre and you used the work books to refresh your memory or take notes from to assist you in your testimony? Is that what you're saying?

utterances.speaker: SIMO ZARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: My investigator could have looked at these work materials, as to what is there, and there were not many topics that I didn't know about, if it was whether this was Zivko Dosen, whether it was Dragan Jakovljevic, whether it was a name which I couldn't quite recall or whether it's Mr. Jeremic, if this I couldn't quite recall, if I was asking for that information, I didn't think that this was any big problem, for me, nor was it presented by my investigator as being some conspiratorial, crucial elements. It wasn't as if anybody said, "here we go, Simo Zaric has decided to write something that he thought of." Mr. Re, I wrote a book to the best of my recollection.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You're not answering the question. The question is quite simple. The question is: Did your investigators bring your work books to the Hague, to the detention centre, for your use during your testimony?

utterances.speaker: SIMO ZARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. They only looked at what's written in there and then they would give me this information. If there was any clarification that I needed or if I had any need to write to them, then I would write it down and send it to them.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Back to my earlier question, where are these work books now?

utterances.speaker: SIMO ZARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Why? Do you want to carry out a search?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I don't want the precise location.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: No, Mr. Zaric, you can just answer the question.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It's in a safe place.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Zaric, those work books would contain one of the best sources of information as to what actually happened at Bosanski Samac during 1992 and 1993, wouldn't they? Because you were recording them, recording the major events in your work books, in hundreds of work books, as you went.

utterances.speaker: SIMO ZARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. Hundreds of -- not hundreds of work books but hundreds of topics, not hundreds of work books.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. Well, hundreds of topics in a number of work books, but you were recording these things as you went on a daily basis. Now they would contain, wouldn't they, one of the best sources of information about what happened in Bosanski Samac during the war, 1992 and 1993, wouldn't they, Mr. Zaric?

utterances.speaker: SIMO ZARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I always kept to a saying among our people, is that crazy person remembers, a wise person writes things down. I was always trying to write everything down so that I could remember, and of course what I needed was there, and before I left for The Hague, and in my preparations I was going over my notes, recalling what was in them but there wasn't very much that I couldn't recall and if there was anything really necessary for me to recall, then I did it in the way that I've already described to you.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you know of any better source of recorded history in Bosanski Samac as to what happened during the war than your work books?

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: This is speculation, I believe. How could he know whether there is any better source?

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: He may know. He may know who wrote the definitive history of Bosanski Samac based upon his work books. I don't know. I wasn't there.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I don't know about that. I know that there are many people who wrote all kinds of things. They wrote books, they wrote notes. Whether anyone was more pedantic than I was and whether the source of information in different military institutions and authorities, how it was kept, recorded, filed, I don't know about that. I can only assume that others in a similar way worked just like me, whoever wanted to be conscientious about their work, and there is also people who just sat and listened and there are people who didn't dealt with this in this way.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The book you wrote, the very last page of it says, "In Belgrade, 24 hours before my departure for The Hague." Do we take it from that that you wrote the book, or finished it, in Belgrade, 24 hours before your departure for The Hague?.

utterances.speaker: SIMO ZARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Where does it say that? Can you show it to me?

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: I believe that by a slight look at the original --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Re?

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Your Honour, if I may have the floor?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Maybe, I'm looking at the original of this book, on the cover page, on the last page, there are words, "In Belgrade, 24 hours before I leave to The Hague," but it doesn't relate to the book when it was written but to this very short text. It's a letter, a statement, letter he wrote 24 hours before he surrendered and this is on the last page so -- with a photograph of his wife and son, so it doesn't says that the book was written and finally written 24 hours before he decided to surrender himself.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Re?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WILLIAMS
utterances.text: If I could just interject, I was going to say it was my recollection that Mr. Zaric surrendered to The Hague, he was here and this book was published in 1999 when he was on provisional release or something like that. If my understanding is correct. Is that so, Mr. Zaric?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No. Not during provisional release but you're right that the book was written in 1999 and it was promoted in Belgrade. That's true, Your Honour, but not at that time. It was 19th of April, 2000, that I was provisionally released. 19th of April, 2000.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The back cover of the book which Mr. Lazarevic or Mr. Pisarevic has in his hand says, "all the details in my confession," meaning the book, "are based on information that can be checked and proved. They are real and true and will remain so after The Hague regardless of what my fate may be." It goes on a bit. And at the bottom it says, "In Belgrade, 24 hours before my departure for The Hague."

utterances.speaker: SIMO ZARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: What's contestable here?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Nothing. But you've appended -- I'm just saying that you've appended to the back of the book a letter in which you say all the details in it are based on information that can be checked and proved, real and true, and remain so after The Hague, and you did so before you went to The Hague.

utterances.speaker: SIMO ZARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I wish to say to the Trial Chamber, the large part, the majority of the documents that I mentioned here on the last page is been authentically processed and given to the committee for investigation of war crimes in Belgrade, and they handed that over to The Hague office of the -- to the Belgrade office of the Hague Tribunal and on the basis of these documents that my organ worked when I was a morale officer, it is on the basis of these notes that people from Odzak and Orasje are being prosecuted in courts regarding the events there but the authentic documentation and I meant what my learned lawyer gave to this honourable court and to the Prosecutor's Office, because that's what the agreement was before the trial even began.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: It's 10.30, Your Honour. Is it time for the break?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes, I just want to say, Mr. Re, can we go back to the indictment, the allegations, the evidence this witness has given? Proceeding in this manner questioning behind how he wrote this book and where his notes are and things like that, the Trial Chamber thinks are not helpful. You've spent quite a lot of time on that.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Of course.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: We will take our break now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Re.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Zaric, we were speaking about your book just before the break, and the letter which is written on the back in which you say that everything in the book is real and true and was attached to the back of the book, the published version. I just want to take you to something in the book and it's where you refer at -- you refer to --

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: I apologise, this quotation is not correct. This letter at the moment when this letter was written by Mr. Zaric but I don't want to give testimony instead of him. The quotation was not right. It is not in this book -- it is not in this letter, not one single word that says everything that is in this book is correct. And maybe Mr. Zaric could read out the last page of the book.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Mr. Re, why are we still continuing on this? Can we please go back to the allegations against the accused?

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: That's exactly what I'm doing, Your Honour. I'm doing that. I don't understand. I'm doing that. I was asking a question and Mr. Lazarevic started testifying.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: The allegation inside the book?

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Of course, the book is full of matters relevant to the indictment. I just want to go into that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Mr. Lazarevic?

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Your Honour, I will repeat my submission. Can Mr. Zaric take a look at this? Is there is nothing referring to the book in this letter. Mr. Re just said to Mr. Zaric, in this last page, in this letter, you say that everything that is in the book is correct and true. And this is not what is written here. So I'm just kindly asking him to show this to Mr. Zaric and that he can read out what it says here. All the details from my notebook, from this book or whatever, from my -- how should I put it? It is not a statement. From my -- he used a very particular version.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Can we have the book given to Mr. Zaric himself and maybe he can explain?

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Zaric, I have an official translation of the back cover of your book in my hands.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Why can't he read the relevant passage?

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Mr. Lazarevic is contesting the translation. It won't be in the --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: We have the interpreters.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: That's right, but it won't be a translation; it will be an interpretation. That's the difficulty. I have an official translation here. All Mr. Zaric will do is read something which is inevitably going to be different to the official translation. And Mr. Lazarevic appears to be contesting for the first time the official translation of the back page. Of course he can read it out. I'm just pointing out that there will be a difference between what he says and is interpreted back to us and what the translation says.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Let Mr. Zaric himself read that and explain what it means.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Sure.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The text is rather short. So I would like to read it out in order for the Trial Chamber to have an insight into it. "All the details from my confession are based on facts which can be checked and proved. They are real and true, and will remain such even after The Hague, independently of what my fate will be. They are my strictest judge because they are the true truth, as said. The judgement, whatever it may be, will be only the result of the attitude toward that truth. Fortunately, the truth cannot be altered. But unfortunately, it can be understood and interpreted in different ways. As you read this, you too are part of the jury that will decide on the truth. Hard and binding words can be covered as said only by a pure and honest man. I have had to check the truth in The Hague, to certify the truth in The Hague, in Belgrade, 24 hours before my departure for The Hague. In the last part of the book, you will see that I have entered some corrections by hand and this is what I tried to say in this book."

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can I ask how that's any different to what I read to the witness before? There seems to be some contesting of the official translation which appears to be almost identical to what Mr. Zaric read out?

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: No. The truth is, the question as you posed it suggests that this is related to the book, that this letter is related to this particular book. First of all, Mr. Zaric used a word --

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: I object. If you're going to clue the witness I object to it.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: I really don't want to give any testimony instead of Mr. Zaric. Please just ask when this letter was written and for what reason and in relation to what.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Mr. Re? You're not going to continue the --

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: No, I don't want to. I don't understand what all that was about.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Go ahead with the cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: It's all right, Madam usher, you may sit down, he probably will need to refer to the book, if my learned friends don't mind Mr. Zaric having your copy, we have other copies but if you're happy with that, we can leave that one there with him.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: We will keep this for redirect.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Zaric, in your book I just want to take you to a passage, if you can just pick up your book or maybe you remember. It's just toward the end the last few pages where you're referring to an interview that you had with a Croatian media outlet and there is a question and answer process. So the last few pages. Around about, I think, page 266 to 267 of your book.

utterances.speaker: SIMO ZARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes? Please tell me what you want me to comment on.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The first one is a question from the Croatian media outlet. What you've done is you have -- I think it's about page 266, you have set out the question and the answer, question and answer, question and answer, based upon the transcript. Have you found it?

utterances.speaker: SIMO ZARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I have come to this part of the book where the journalist from Serbia who worked for a Croatian newspaper was asking me questions, just tell me what question interests you and what my answer was in the book.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The first question, 243 of the English, Question: "Do you admit that there was ethnic cleansing?"

utterances.speaker: SIMO ZARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Answer: "Of course there was. Take Odzak for example. Across the river from Samac. Dozens of Odzak Serbs were killed, more than 800 were tortured in prisons and camps, many Serb women were raped. Not one of the 6.000 Serbs who lived in the municipality remains there now. My family used to live there too, but it's gone. The house where I was born was among the first to be burned and demolished. I can give you hundreds of such examples in Bosnia-Herzegovina or across the river in Croatia." Next question: "I was asking you about ethnic cleansing in Samac!" Answer: "I know very well what you wanted me to say, so yes, there was but on both sides. I am not trying to establish an artificial symmetry because I don't want anyone to answer for this, but as soon as it was decided that separation would be ethnically based, and effected by means of war, this kind of symmetry was inevitable. Does it matter at all who started it? Or who started it with a little ethnic cleansing and later did a little more -- or sorry, a little bit more ethnic cleansing, whether it was done in order to settle old accounts or because the concepts chosen could not be realised otherwise?" I won't read the whole thing. It goes down to just before the next question. I want to stress that if there are no Croats and Muslims here, and no Serbs there, both are instances of ethnic cleansing. If there is guilt here, there is guilt there, as well. Therefore no nation, including the Serb nation, can let such things pass without a sense of frustration and huge injustice if either side is amnestied in advance. I've read correctly what you wrote in your book, based upon questions and answers to a Serbian person or Serbian journalist working for a Croatian newspaper, didn't I?

utterances.speaker: SIMO ZARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. You have read my reply.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And that's your view, isn't it, that there was ethnic cleansing in Bosanski Samac and both sides were guilty of ethnic cleansing, Croats and Serbs?

utterances.speaker: SIMO ZARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. That's my conviction.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Zaric, in your work in or as a member of the JNA reserve, or the SDB reserve and your years of association with the security services, you were aware of the structure of the security services and the JNA in the former Yugoslavia, before April, 1992, weren't you?

utterances.speaker: SIMO ZARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I don't know exactly what the structure of the security service was in the JNA, but I know for certain that care was taken to make sure that at the top, in the administration, and in key positions, representatives of all ethnic groups making up Yugoslavia should be present.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Before the withdrawal of the JNA or the formal withdrawal of the JNA in May, 1992, the command structure went from the federal Presidency of the SFRY downwards through the federal Secretary for National Defence, didn't it?

utterances.speaker: SIMO ZARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And the federal Secretary for National Defence in -- at the end of 1991 and the beginning of 1992, was Colonel General Veljko Kadijevic, wasn't it?

utterances.speaker: SIMO ZARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And the chief of general staff reported directly to him, correct?

utterances.speaker: SIMO ZARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know what the method of work was but I assume that's how it should have been.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: At the level below the federal Secretary for National Defence, that is at the beginning of 1992, Colonel General Kadijevic, there was the deputy SSNO, the chief of general staff, the assistant to the SSNO, that's the federal Secretary for National Defence, the head of intelligence, that was Colonel General Aleksandar Vasiljevic and the chief of cabinet for the federal Secretary of National Defence?

utterances.speaker: SIMO ZARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as I can remember, the federal Secretary for National Defence was Colonel General Veljko Kadijevic, who was born in a mixed marriage. His father was a Croat, his mother was Serb. His deputy was Stane Brovet --

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Please, we are not interested in the ethnicity of the people concerned. Please concentrate. I'm asking you about the structure. All I'm saying is I read to you some positions, they were directly below Kadijevic in the hierarchy, including of course Colonel General Aleksandar Vasiljevic, the head of the UB or military intelligence?

utterances.speaker: SIMO ZARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. But I want to say that it's very important that the deputy was Stane Brovet, a Slovene, and that the chief of the general staff was Mr. Blagoje Adzic, and that the chief of the administration for security was Aco Vasiljevic. Those were the people I was aware of at the time.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you, and the JNA before it withdrew from Bosnia formally was divided into five districts reporting to the -- or four military districts or five districts in all, reporting to the federal Secretary for National Defence, namely the 1st Military District, in Belgrade, the 3rd Military District in Skopje, the 5th Military District in Zagreb, the Naval Military District in Split, and the RVIPVO, which is the air force and air defence which was led by Colonel General Zvonko Jurjevic. Those were the five divisions of the JNA before the withdrawal from Bosnia, weren't they?

utterances.speaker: SIMO ZARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. This was before the outbreak of the war on the territory of the former Yugoslavia, and you forgot to mention that there was also the 2nd Military District with its headquarters in Sarajevo, but all this was before the secession of Croatia and Slovenia from Yugoslavia. The structure you are talking about is familiar to me from the time before the secessionist policy of Slovenia and Croatia and I agree with you that that is what it looked like more or less at the level of the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The 1st Military District in Belgrade, that was at that time, 1991 and early 1992 was commanded by Colonel General Zivota Panic, correct?

utterances.speaker: SIMO ZARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's possible. I don't know about him. But of course I have heard of him. He was later the chief of the federal Secretary for National Defence but I do know that the command of the 2nd Military District in Bosnia-Herzegovina was Colonel General or Lieutenant General Milutin Kukanjac. I know this because he was directly connected to Bosnia and Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The division of responsibility at that time was that the 1st Military District in Belgrade was responsible for the part of Bosnia-Herzegovina where you were stationed. That is the end of 1991 and up to May, 1992, when the JNA withdrew? And General Panic was the commander between September 1991 and May, 1992?

utterances.speaker: SIMO ZARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I didn't understand you properly. Could you please repeat your question? Because General Panic had nothing to do with us in Bosnia.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The 1st Military District, its headquarters were in Belgrade, its commander was General Panic from September 1991 to May 1992, the 17th Corps commanded by Major General Savo Jankovic who appointed you to your position, was subordinated to General Panic in Belgrade, wasn't it?

utterances.speaker: SIMO ZARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, no. You are not correct. If you want, I will give you a precise explanation.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, if the commander of the 17th Corps was not subordinated to the 1st Military District, just tell us who he was subordinated to, please, without a lengthy explanation, just the name of the division. Sorry, the name of the district where it was headquartered.

utterances.speaker: SIMO ZARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The commander of the 17th Corps of the JNA headquartered in Tuzla was General Savo Jankovic and he was subordinated to the command of the 2nd Military District headquartered in Sarajevo at whose head was Lieutenant General Milutin Kukanjac.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, the -- you were aware that the JNA in 1991 and 1992, formed operational groups?

utterances.speaker: SIMO ZARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as I know, there were tactical groups but it is possible that operational groups exist in the army. I know about tactical groups and the 17th Tactical Group which was established for our area, including the area of Bosanski Samac.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, I suggest there were operational groups which were reporting directly to the JNA general staff in Belgrade and they were the Operational Group 1, in Western Slavonia, Operational Group 2 in Mostar, Split, Dubrovnik, Operational Group 3 in Eastern Slavonia, Operational Group 5 in Banija, Kordun and Lika.

utterances.speaker: SIMO ZARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: To be quite honest, I have no idea about these operational groups or the methods as to who and how they reported to. In the military, Simo Zaric was assistant commander of the 4th Detachment which was part of the 17th Tactical Group.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: There were operational groups in the Krajina area which included special police units commanded by Commander Borjevic [phoen], weren't there?

utterances.speaker: SIMO ZARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I hear this last name for the first time here. I don't know how operational groups or units were formed in the Krajina or elsewhere.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I'm asking about your awareness as someone who worked in military intelligence and appointed to that position by General Jankovic of the special police units in the Krajina that were part of the JNA operational group?

utterances.speaker: SIMO ZARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: General Jankovic had nothing to do with what was happening across the River Sava in the Republic of Croatia, nor did he have anything to do with what was happening on the territory of the Republic of Srpska Krajina, where the Serbs for a while kept a certain area under control. He was the commander of the 2nd Corps connected to Tuzla and the broader region of Bosnia and Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you not understand my question? My question was directed at your awareness. My question was: I'm asking you about your awareness of -- as someone who worked in military intelligence and were appointed to that position by General Jankovic, your awareness of special police units in the Krajina that were part of the JNA operational groups, Banija, Kordun. I want you to tell the Trial Chamber about your awareness of the special police units in the Krajina.

utterances.speaker: SIMO ZARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honours, there is no link whatsoever that I may have had with this information, nor did I have any task when I was appointed and proposed to work for a while as a person who would be gathering security intelligence information in the area of Posavina, more precisely the three municipalities where before the war I had been a chief of the state security service. Now, my range and my information were only to do with this micro location and if I had had any awareness, any knowledge in relation to what Mr. Re is asking me I would gladly answer but really I have absolutely no idea about it, nor was that my task, nor was that ever a topic of conversation between me and Mr. Jankovic regarding this broad subject.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: There is evidence before this Trial Chamber from Colonel Nikolic and you've told the Trial Chamber about this information yourself, that the paramilitaries were or he told you were police from the Krajina. Now, are you saying based upon your last answer that as far as you're concerned, Colonel Nikolic's information about where they came from was wrong? And they weren't special police from the Krajina? Or from somewhere else?

utterances.speaker: SIMO ZARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The information that these specials were kind of connection with the police of the Republika Srpska Krajina, I received sometime in April when they arrived in this area, so anything preceding this period, as to their training, where it was, I had no idea about it, nor did Mr. Nikolic have any idea about it so it's not contested. It's after I received this information and when Mr. Nikolic had a conversation with them on the 12th of April, in Donji Zabar, told us where they came from, and what they told him. I do not contest this information but it has nothing to do with me allegedly having any information about this preceding this event.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: There is a small correction in the transcript but it changes meaning of what Mr. Zaric said. On page 43 line 25, here it says, "I had idea about it" and he said, "I had no idea about it, nor did Mr. Nikolic."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes, we will accept that correction.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Nikolic said that he had seen their ID, they were bearing ID as police from the SAO Krajina. Did you see any of the ID yourself?

utterances.speaker: SIMO ZARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I did not have an opportunity to see that. I heard this from Lieutenant Colonel Nikolic and to be honest, I did not doubt that he had reason, any reason, to make this up, and then tell us this.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You've said that the 17th Corps was based in Tuzla. Now, Tuzla of course had a majority Muslim population, didn't it?

utterances.speaker: SIMO ZARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I don't have a very precise statistical information. I know there was no area in Bosnia-Herzegovina that was not multi-ethnic but how varied the multi-ethnic structures were, I don't know, but I don't exclude the possibility that Tuzla statistically speaking perhaps had, most predominantly, Muslim population and then Serbs, but I cannot say for sure. I'm not certain.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The situation with the JNA in the second half of 1991 and 1992 and you know this from your own position in military intelligence, was that the JNA was experiencing severe difficulties because of the conflict in -- raging across parts of the former Yugoslavia?

utterances.speaker: SIMO ZARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I agree with you.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
