utterances.text: And you know from your own experience in military intelligence that in July, 1990 -- I'm sorry, up until July, 1991, recruitment was done at a republic level to the JNA? But in July, 1991, the JNA command in Belgrade seized from the Sarajevo headquarters, all documentation relating to conscription and the registers and put it into their own hands?

utterances.speaker: SIMO ZARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know for certain the exact information but I know that according to the Presidency decision of the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia, there was a decision that was issued to dislocate, carry out dislocation of weapons from the warehouse of the Territorial Defence, and to take the military records, as you call them, and to place them as part of the Ministry of Defence files because it was then defined as being a state of emergency, and a possibility of the possession of weapons by the Territorial Defence and their dispersion could bring about the break-up the joint force as it was known to be in the JNA. I don't know whether this information that you gave in July, I don't know whether that is so, but I know that there was a Presidency decision going in that direction passed by the Presidency and by the Supreme Commander of the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... Transcript, I don't know suggest anything but it's still July 1991 and Mr. Zaric was referring to Federal Republic of Yugoslavia which was established later. So maybe there is a need for some clarification, what was the name of the state at that time.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Zaric, you were referring to the SFRY, not the FRY, weren't you, in July --

utterances.speaker: SIMO ZARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was thinking of the federal Federative Republic of Yugoslavia because in 1991, there was no complete secession of Slovenia and Croatia from Yugoslavia, so I remember that those decisions were legitimate, they were brought by the Presidency of the SFRJ. I don't know whether that was at the end of the 1991 or not. I am not completely certain of this data. I don't know when this decision was issued.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. Now, the situation in the JNA in Bosnia between July, 1991 and May 1992, when the JNA formally left the territory of Bosnia, was that after the general command in Belgrade took control of recruiting, it was mainly Serbs who were being recruited to the JNA in Bosnia, wasn't it?

utterances.speaker: SIMO ZARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. That's not true.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, the information I've just suggested to you is coming from a judgement of this Tribunal. It's called the Tadic judgement. It's at paragraph 106 of that judgement. The Trial Chamber has found that, a Trial Chamber of this Tribunal has found that to be the case. What do you say about the ethnic composition of the JNA after July, 1991?

utterances.speaker: SIMO ZARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I am aware that it was precisely in July-August, 1991, it was the President of the Presidency of Bosnia-Herzegovina that publicly, all military conscripts were called up, Muslims and Croats, not to respond to the mobilisation, and this is probably what decided the fact, and brought about the polarisation so that as days went by and months as well, what happened was that the Yugoslav People's Army had increasingly more Serbs, while Croats and Muslims were making, establishing their own paramilitary formations, and did not wish to respond to the calls of the Yugoslav People's Army which at the time was the dominant force also in Bosnia-Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The Tadic judgement says, and you can disagree if you like, I'll put this as a proposition to you, that by early 1992, this is paragraph 108, Serbs who had formerly been 40 per cent of the JNA were 90 per cent of the JNA. You'd agree with that, wouldn't you?

utterances.speaker: SIMO ZARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. That's possible. Because those others did not wish to join Yugoslav People's Army, but then the question is where were these others? I agree that perhaps at the time Yugoslav People's Army had in its ranks 90 per cent of Serbs and possibly 10 or so per cent of Croats and Muslims who lived in Bosnia-Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And the result of the withdrawal of Muslims and Croats from the JNA in Bosnia in 1991 and 1992 meant that the JNA was experiencing a severe manpower shortage, wasn't it? It was running short of troops.

utterances.speaker: SIMO ZARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. This polarisation started as a result of a terrible religious polarisation which was carried out by the leaders of national, nationalistic parties, and at that time, Yugoslav People's Army in this area did not have a shortage of soldiers, it was not preparing for war. If it had a task, it was to prevent the multi-ethnic conflict erupting in the area.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: My question was more directed towards the shortage of troops within the JNA. You'd accept, wouldn't you, and this is again coming from the Tadic judgement at paragraph 110, and based upon your own experience in the JNA at the time, that by early 1992, the JNA was experiencing a severe manpower shortage, wasn't it?

utterances.speaker: SIMO ZARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, no. I would not agree with you on that subject.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. Well, if it wasn't experiencing severe manpower shortage, the deficit of -- caused by the Muslims and Croats no longer being in the JNA was filled by Serbs taking their place, wasn't it?

utterances.speaker: SIMO ZARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Serbs in Bosnia-Herzegovina responded to the mobilisation call of the Yugoslav People's Army for a simple reason that the majority of the Serbs, including myself, we lived for Bosnia-Herzegovina, as an administrative unit, should remain part of Yugoslavia and Yugoslav People's Army was the base of the defence component.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You know that in the second half of 1991, the JNA formed TO units in Serb-populated villages in Bosnia-Herzegovina and supplied them with weapons and uniforms, don't you? And that's in the Tadic judgement at page -- paragraph 106.

utterances.speaker: SIMO ZARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I hear this for the first time. I did not read Mr. Tadic's judgement. The Yugoslav People's Army never did, nor was it up to them, to establish some kind of Territorial Defence. They had their own units that were part of their force but it was after the establishment of Republika Srpska as a state entity, it was through their government and certain organs, that the decision was adopted regarding the establishment and constitution of the Territorial Defence for this entity, but Yugoslav People's Army never established a Territorial Defence. This is the first time I hear about this.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The result of the Muslims and Croats leaving the JNA and the Serb mobilisation was that the JNA started to place increasing reliance upon paramilitary units, didn't it? And again I'm referring to the Tadic judgement and your own observations of your work in military intelligence in Bosnia-Herzegovina in 1991 and 1992.

utterances.speaker: SIMO ZARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. That's not true. And if we are speaking about Samac and if there were 20 or 30 of those paramilitaries and there were several thousand of us in a unit, that's an insignificant per cent. I wouldn't say that was a rule but there were plenty of us from the 17th Tactical Group for the zone of responsibility that we were in charge of.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I'm talking about, for example, Zvornik and Bijeljina. In the first week of April, 1992, and you'd know from your work in military intelligence that Zvornik was taken over by paramilitaries, Arkan's men and Seselj's men on the 31st of March and the 1st of April, 1992?

utterances.speaker: SIMO ZARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Some information in respect of what happened there, I found out later, and I read a lot in the newspapers that there were many similar scenarios as the one that happened in Samac but I also know that in March, 1992, from Croatia, there was a paramilitary formation with Cavka. They came to the Odzak municipality and they did the very same thing in that area and all of the organised defence structures, part of the Muslim and Croatian peoples, they organised themselves as paramilitary formation.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Zaric, you're not seriously saying you didn't know at the time that Arkan and Seselj's men had taken over Zvornik? That's in the first few days of April, 1992. You're not seriously saying that, are you?

utterances.speaker: SIMO ZARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The media followed the situation in particular and I was able to see certain scenes on TV, and it was also later on I found out something directly from people and I know that these kind of forces were involved in the war conflicts in Bijeljina area and in the Zvornik area, but at the time, I did not know what was going on there. Later on, I have -- had had some information regarding this.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Zaric, you knew, in early April, 1992, that paramilitary units had seized control of Zvornik, didn't you? You couldn't not have known in military intelligence in a very -- a matter of 70 kilometres or so away.

utterances.speaker: SIMO ZARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: 150 kilometres from Samac but I really did not know what was going on in Zvornik. But regarding the media, I was able to see what was going on in Bijeljina because that's where Mrs. Biljana Plavsic was with a very similar delegation as it was in Bosanski Brod between the 25th and 26th of March, 1992.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: That's where Mrs. Plavsic was and that's where Arkan went and that's where she greeted him with a kiss, you see that in the media?

utterances.speaker: SIMO ZARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, we all saw that on TV. I'm not contesting that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Of course Arkan was a paramilitary leader, wasn't he?

utterances.speaker: SIMO ZARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: He had his own unit, and the behaviour of that unit, I think, is well known. I had the opportunity to hear and read about what happened not just in Bijeljina but elsewhere, in other areas, where his unit, units went, how much they were paramilitary units or not, I wouldn't go into that but I know that where these units went, there were certain significant problems.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You knew at the time that is in April, early April, 1992, that Arkan's paramilitary unit had taken over, Bijeljina, didn't you? You knew that from the media and from your own intelligence work.

utterances.speaker: SIMO ZARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I was aware of that information, that they managed to contain the situation, and that after that, there was peace for a period in Bijeljina, but where it went afterwards, to which areas, I wouldn't know.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And you know that in both towns, not so far from Bosanski Samac, the JNA did not prevent Arkan or Seselj taking control of those two towns, the JNA did not prevent the paramilitary units from taking control of those towns, and you knew that at the time, didn't you?

utterances.speaker: SIMO ZARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I know that Yugoslav People's Army at the time had a conflict with Arkan in the Bijeljina area. I know that Arkan beat up the commander of the barracks in Bijeljina. He is now Colonel Marsalo [phoen].

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: I believe that the rank of the officer was general. That's what Mr. Zaric said.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] He's now a general. At the time he was a colonel.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Will Your Honours just excuse me for one moment? I'm just looking for something I've mislaid.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You know, Mr. Zaric, and you know from the media and your own intelligence work at the time, that the JNA assisted Arkan in Zvornik by shelling when the paramilitary units went in, don't you?

utterances.speaker: SIMO ZARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know that. And I don't know how I would know that and why are you linking me to the area which was 150 kilometres away from me? If you want me to tell you what I read in newspaper articles, I don't know how important that is for this Trial Chamber.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When these paramilitary units arrived in Bosanski Samac -- sorry, in Pelagicevo -- Batkusa on about the 11th of April, 1992, it was after the takeover of Bijeljina and Zvornik by similar paramilitary units, wasn't it?

utterances.speaker: SIMO ZARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. That happened after that, but I have the information what happened in Bijeljina before Arkan came to Bijeljina but I don't think that is something that is important for us to discuss before this Trial Chamber.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You, and all the other members of your command, were aware that the paramilitaries had taken over towns in Bosanski Samac before they arrived in Batkusa, weren't you?

utterances.speaker: SIMO ZARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I know that.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: There is a problem -- I believe here there is something in the transcript that is maybe that the question was not properly recorded. Here it says you and all the other members of your command, were aware that the paramilitaries had taken over towns in Bosanski Samac before they arrived in Batkusa. This is what it says. It was the transcript says so it's most probably not properly recorded.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: If there is any ambiguity, what I meant was members of Serbian paramilitary units, not the ones who arrived in Batkusa, not those particular ones but members of similar Serbian paramilitary units, had already taken over towns in Bosanski Samac -- sorry, in Bosnia-Herzegovina. I think your answer was, referring to your interpretation of my question, was you knew that.

utterances.speaker: SIMO ZARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I know that Bijeljina happened before Samac, but I also know that before Arkan's arrival, the Green Berets turned up there and caused an incident and that the Public Security Service was not able to deal with it, and that several young men of Serb nationality were killed in those conflicts, and that's probably when Mr. Arkan came and did what he did, and then Bijeljina was put under some sort of control. Arkan withdrew and Bijeljina never experienced any further war.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: But of course this was the same Arkan who committed summary executions of a large number of Muslims within a week of arriving there, wasn't it?

utterances.speaker: SIMO ZARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I learned this information from the media.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: That information was well known at the time the paramilitaries arrived in Batkusa, wasn't it?

utterances.speaker: SIMO ZARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know how well known it was, but I know what I saw in the media, and I said that I was able to see on television the arrival of Mrs. Plavsic and her exchange of kisses with Arkan and information also arrived that the situation there was under control. As for the number of dead, I learned that later, that information was not given out right away. I do not exclude the possibility that what was published in the newspapers was not correct, and that several lads of Muslim ethnicity were killed after Arkan came to Bijeljina.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, it was 20 on the 9th of April, 1992. Does that jog your memory? 20 Bosnian Muslim and Croat men and boys who were detained by Arkan's men in Zvornik. Does that date assist you? It was the 9th of April, 1992.

utterances.speaker: SIMO ZARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was not possible for us to get information of that kind so quickly in Samac as to know how many people were killed in Bijeljina or in Zvornik. It was two days later that these people came to us. The information was not so precise, nor did anyone try to broadcast this sort of information in public. So I had no idea how many people exactly were killed, either in Zvornik or in Bijeljina.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The situation was that you and the other members of the 4th Detachment command and military intelligence within the 17th Tactical Group were aware that paramilitary -- Serbian paramilitary groups were taking over towns and committing atrocities before the takeover in Bosanski Samac on the 16th and 17th of April, 1992?

utterances.speaker: SIMO ZARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I understand, Mr. Re, what direction you're going in but it was not possible for us to have this information at that time. If this happened as you say on the 9th of April, and these people came to us two days later, do you think somebody ran to us right away to tell us this and this happened, so many people were killed? How could I know about certain massacres and certain incidents that happened hundreds of kilometres away? This was simply impossible. It can't be understood in this way. It did not go through the Internet.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Your command and the members of military intelligence in the 17th Tactical Group were aware, including yourself, of the takeovers by paramilitaries in other towns in Bosnia before the takeover in Bosanski Samac? You can't deny that, can you?

utterances.speaker: SIMO ZARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I know about Bijeljina, I didn't hear about Zvornik. I know about Bosanski Brod because that was after the Croats took over. I know about Odzak and areas that were closer to us and the surroundings of Samac but as to what happened on other territories, I learned that in the course of the war and I read quite a lot about it after the war. At that time, however, there was no way I could have known this. I know what happened in the immediate vicinity. This is the information I feel at home with and that you can ask me about as much as you like.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So you're saying the information from -- about the takeover of Zvornik on the 31st of March and the 1st of April and Bijeljina a week later, by paramilitary groups within the JNA's area of responsibility didn't filter through to the 17th Tactical Group's --

utterances.speaker: SIMO ZARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm not hearing the interpretation, Mr. Re, I apologise. I can't hear you.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Are you getting it now? Is everyone clearly getting it?

utterances.speaker: SIMO ZARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know who knew what at a that level but as for me, as the assistant commander of the detachment in Samac, I did not have this information at my disposal. Whether someone at the level of the 17th Corps had that information, well, that's possible, but it did not filter down to the level of Simo Zaric, who was assistant commander at the level of the 4th Detachment. There were no hostilities of that kind and that complexity in our neck of the woods at the time.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Zaric, your evidence to the Trial Chamber last week was that General Jankovic personally appointed you to gather intelligence and report to Maksimovic, Nikolic, and if necessary him, about what was happening on the ground. Now, the evidence has been that Nikolic informed his command, that is, Jankovic, that the paramilitaries had arrived. Are you seriously telling the Trial Chamber that Nikolic, Jankovic, Maksimovic, none of them said to you, "Look, Zaric, we've had takeovers in other towns by paramilitary units from Serbia, Zvornik, Bijeljina, Bosanski Brod. Some have landed in our area. You better keep an eye on them." Nothing like that happened? No mention of these takeovers by paramilitaries very similar to those who arrived in the Bosanski Samac area?

utterances.speaker: SIMO ZARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Re, I cannot accept what you say. I was the assistant commander of a detachment. It was my task to gather basic information in that area and hand it over to my immediate superior whose name was Makso Simeunovic. I had only one or two contacts. My first contact with General Jankovic, he did not appoint me but it was agreed on during the conversation that I was to perform intelligence tasks and that before the war, I was to collect information for the 17th Tactical Group and I was not the one who went and submitted reports to General Jankovic directly. My level of work was to report only to my immediate superior of the information I passed on to him, what he passed on further to the 17th Corps, I never entered into that. As for feedback of the kind that you are talking about, it never reached me. I heard about this from the media more than it was a topic of conversation in the way that you are trying to get me to confirm. I cannot confirm this because I did not know it.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So you're basically saying that no one in the command of the 17th Tactical Group or the 17th Corps passed on any information to you that you should look out for these paramilitaries because they might be attempting a takeover like they had in other towns? Just no discussion of that at all, no mention of Serbian paramilitaries and taking over towns and being dangerous men? Nothing? Is that what you're saying?

utterances.speaker: SIMO ZARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: When I submitted my intelligence information as to what was going on in the area, I gave so much exhaustive information during my examination-in-chief, and this was information I had at my disposal that I submitted to my immediate superior. What the methods were of distributing information from the 17th Tactical Group upwards, I cannot say that, because I was not a participant in that, and no one gave me feedback except that I was told that I should continue gathering information and submitted it. That's what my superior told me and that's what I did in a disciplined manner.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So what you're saying is completely suggestive of the fact that the local JNA command, Nikolic, Jankovic, et cetera, weren't concerned about the arrival of the paramilitaries, if they didn't pass on information to you that these similar groups had taken over other towns? That's the only conclusion you can draw from that, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: SIMO ZARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I agree with you that perhaps they were deeply concerned about these issues. They were serious people and I don't believe that this sort of information bypassed people in the top leadership of the JNA. I don't know what they talked about among themselves but I do agree with you that it is realistic to assume that they would have been concerned about the situation in their area of responsibility.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, when the Prosecutor asked you in the interview on the 1st of April, which is P140 ter, at page 53, the question, Nancy, "wasn't it a fact that these paramilitary groups you referred to were under the command of the JNA before the attack?" And your answer was, "You'll have to ask Mr. Nikolic."

utterances.speaker: SIMO ZARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's what I said, yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And you said that because you know that they were under JNA command but you just didn't want to put it in the record of the interview.

utterances.speaker: SIMO ZARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's your conclusion.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, I'm asking you to comment on it. I'm suggesting that's the reason why you said that. You didn't say they weren't. You said you'll have to ask Mr. Nikolic, it's a rather cryptic answer to a fairly straight question, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: SIMO ZARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. In both of my interviews, I explained the reasons why I thought so. That one sentence doesn't mean anything because Mr. Nikolic told us at one point, when we told him that we thought this was a gang doing certain things, he initially agreed with that, and then he said that he would do his best to find out what this was all about and to put it under control as far as was possible. To what extent Mr. Nikolic put this under his control or not, well, that's why I said to Madam Nancy Paterson if that's important, ask Mr. Nikolic, and he was -- he testified before this Trial Chamber.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Of course, if you turn the page over, you'll see what you went on to say, that's at page 54, when the Prosecutor went on to say, "you know nothing about that," I won't read the part on page 53, I'll go to the top of page 54, the part that starts, I'll just wait until you find it, "I would like to say that on the first day." Maybe it's on page 55. It's page 54. And it's -- it's in Bosnian, about a third of the way down the page.

utterances.speaker: SIMO ZARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I have page 54 before me.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. Just read along with me. Your answer to the question or part of your answer to the question, "you know nothing about that," after you've explained about the arrival, the top of that page, you say, "I would like to say that on the first day, information came that these people, this group of people, drank heavily, that they also stopped buses, that they robbed people. I personally asked Commander Nikolic what should be done about this. He said that his perception... I said how come that these people who arrived were such people? He said that his perception was that this was some kind of a gang and he would take care of them." What you then said, Mr. Zaric, was, "and after a couple of days, that changed and he said that he was putting them under his command. "Now, I would like to tell you, Mrs. Nancy, that the way I saw Mr. Nikolic, until that very moment, I always saw him as a great Yugoslav, and when that happened, and the arrival of that group, then I saw that he couldn't possibly keep them under his control."

utterances.speaker: SIMO ZARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Everything here is correct. Yes. As far as I'm concerned. And I abide by what I said.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: That is that Nikolic told you he was putting them under his command several days after they arrived and before the takeover of Bosanski Samac?

utterances.speaker: SIMO ZARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I didn't say under command. I said under control. And these are two quite different things. He said he would try to put this under control. This does not mean that he was supposed to command them. He explained what his idea was. He invited them for an interview. He wanted to see them. He informed his superior command and received certain instructions and orders as to how he should treat them. Let's not repeat Mr. Nikolic's testimony before this Trial Chamber.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Maybe there is some problem with the translation of this document. The official translation was done years ago and it has never been objected to by your counsel or anyone else. Your counsel has never objected to the words which are in the English, "And after a couple of days, that changed and he said that he was putting them under his command." That's what it says.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Yes, and here on B/C/S it says that he will put them "under his control and that we shouldn't not worry about it." This is what we are reading in B/C/S, on page 54 of this document.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Well, I --

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Of course Mr. Zaric can read this out in B/C/S.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: I press the Prosecution's position that this document has been in evidence for a long time, the Defence have had it for a long time and it's formed part of the exhibit in this case and no one has ever challenged that translation of what is a very important aspect of both cases, one would think, until this second. Is the Defence asking for it to be retranslated?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Except to note that, Mr. Re, the same paragraph on page 54, when you continue reading it, the accused continues to say, "now I would like to tell you, Mrs. Nancy," if you begin from there, the end it shows that, "I saw that he couldn't possibly keep them under his control."

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: I read that to Mr. Zaric, there are two concepts there, Your Honour. One is command and one is control. Your Honours know about de facto and de jure issues in the military.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: As a matter of fact this is not the first time that this very same part of the --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Lazarevic?

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Yes, if I may suggest one word, Your Honour, I believe that it was during cross-examination of one of the witnesses, frankly I -- my memory is not that good, but I believe that it was Mr. Weiner who cross-examined one of the witnesses and this very same problem appeared at that moment because I objected again because I always quoted Mr. Zaric interview as keeping things under control, and what I believe would be the easiest way is to just show it and ask Mr. Zaric to read out in B/C/S what he actually said, and in B/C/S it says there are two actually sentences mentioning what Mr. Nikolic said to them, whether it's under command or under control, and in B/C/S n both sentences, it is said under control, to keep things under control. While looking here and at English version, it is true that it says, under his command, on sentence one and on the other one, under control. So this is basically what it is. But I believe that Mr. Zaric was speaking in B/C/S and giving answers in B/C/S.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: But is the B/C/S word different, one for command and one for control?

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Just like in English, control and command are two different things.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WILLIAMS
utterances.text: Yes, but is the -- unfortunately I've only got the English one in front of me but is the word that is used the same word or are there two words used in the B/C/S version?

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Your Honour, these are two words, "komanda" and "kontrola," very similar to the English in B/C/S. And of course in B/C/S, Mr. Zaric used both times words "control" both times, in both sentences, "kontrola."

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: I'm no expert but I can clearly see "komandi" and "kontrolom" in that paragraph below, the 7th line from the bottom, "Nikolic je nama rekao u komandi tada maltene da." And in the last line, "Drzi pod svojom kontrolom." There is of course an audio of this interview, if there is any doubt as to what Mr. Zaric actually said.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: I hope so but the Prosecution is the one that provided us with the copies of the interview and the translation. Mr. Zaric can simply read out what is in B/C/S. [Defence counsel confer].

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, if I may be of assistance.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Zaric?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I assert that the tape can be reviewed and I assert that I used the word "control" on both -- in both sentences. I never said put under his command. I have been able to look at the or listen to the audio tape and to see the B/C/S transcript. In both cases, I used the word "control". I never said he was putting him under his command. That is my definitive reply to this so we need not waste time on it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes, would and we can ask the registry to give us the correct interpretation. They will use the audiotapes.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: I'm sure we can clarify that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: But in your -- just hang on for one moment. In the interview of June, 1998 at page 22, that's P142 ter -- have you found it? Halfway down the page, "So who is responsible for the takeover of Samac?"

utterances.speaker: SIMO ZARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Olga says "the Crisis Staff and the SDS. The SDS were responsible," apparently translating your words; is that correct, that Olga has just used your words, "the Crisis Staff and the SDS, the authorities were responsible?" Just asking you if Olga has just repeated what you said in the line before.

utterances.speaker: SIMO ZARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: John, a lawyer, repeats, "The Crisis Staff was responsible," and Olga repeats it and you answer or Olga answers for you, she says, "that is my deep conviction and I think the part of the responsibility can also be taken by the command of the 17th Tactical Group. I am talking about Mr. Nikolic. But what happened later showed that as soon as the Yugoslav People's Army left the territory of Bosnia and Herzegovina, only a few days after the war began, that SDS components of the war option prepared in its own way." Not once --

utterances.speaker: SIMO ZARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know what you want from me.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I just want you to read it. Having read it, not once but twice you referred to Mr. Nikolic in the context of responsibility for the takeover.

utterances.speaker: SIMO ZARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. And do you want me to comment on what I said?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Maybe not now.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: It's 12.30. Is that the time for the break?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes. We will take our break and continue at 1250 hours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Re. You continue.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Zaric, I was asking you before the break about the -- your references to Mr. Nikolic or Colonel Nikolic as he then was, Lieutenant Colonel Nikolic, in the context of your attributing some responsibility to him for the takeover. Now, when you said, "That is my deep conviction and I think that part of the responsibility had also be taken by the command of the 17th Tactical Group, I'm talking about Mr. Nikolic," that is at page 23 of P142, which I read to you before and you read yourself, what you're saying there is that you regarded Nikolic and the 17th Tactical Group as being responsible for the takeover in the same way that the paramilitaries were, don't you? That's what those words mean.

utterances.speaker: SIMO ZARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm going to tell you what my words mean.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You're going to tell me they mean something else, are you?

utterances.speaker: SIMO ZARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Absolutely.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. Okay, then. What do the words "I think part of the responsibility can also be taken by the command of the 17th Tactical Group and I'm talking about Mr. Nikolic" mean, if not what they say?

utterances.speaker: SIMO ZARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I said that it could be attributed to them. That's how I said it. That word is not too strict in that sense but when I said that, my starting point was that as far as we were concerned, Mr. Nikolic told us that he would make certain efforts in order to place this group under his control and so on, and even today my conviction is, although I believe Mr. Nikolic to be a very conscientious officer, whether he on his side had done everything that he could to place this group that had said that belonged to the police but whether, in according to the position that he had as the commander of the 17th Tactical Group, whether he did enough in order to place this group under his control, it is within this context that I looked at. Perhaps that's a cursory assessment but that's how I felt it, and that's the reason why I said that Mr. Nikolic would have this part of some kind of responsibility but whether he was able to do anything or not, I'm just assuming that somehow through his position, he was able to come to more precise data who these people were, perhaps to make more of an effort to either place them more under more of a control or something else. That's what I said. But I'm not putting this on the same level as the specials who were taking over the town. I'm not placing them on the same level as the 17th Tactical Group or units of the Yugoslav People's Army.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Zaric, thank you for the explanation. I just want to take you to P127, which is the 13 signatories document which of course is reproduced in full in your book and which you told the Trial Chamber last week that you had spent several months gathering information and intelligence on the document before you prepared it.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Could the witness perhaps be shown P127, please?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I never said anywhere that I was working on this for several months.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I think your evidence was that you took several months to gather the information necessary to --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: I think Mr. Re the evidence is on record. Just proceed.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Zaric, I take you to the third paragraph on the first page, the one that starts, "Second." "Second, even while the tactical group or TG17 existed and Lieutenant Colonel Nikolic was here, a group of so-called 'Serbian commandos' led by Crni and Debeli arrived in this area in a military helicopter. Nikolic and the 17th Tactical Group command initially branded it as a 'paramilitary group' and a 'group of bandits and mercenaries,' but after only five or six days, they endorsed it and explained it as a 'legal elite unit of Serbian commandos' whose arrival had been legalised through the official organs of government and the army both at the level of Samac municipality and at the highest level in Serbia and Yugoslavia." Now that document was of course -- sorry, you prepared that document relatively contemporaneously compared to when you gave your statements to the Prosecutor some six years later. You agree with that?

utterances.speaker: SIMO ZARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I didn't understand you very well.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: This document is far more contemporaneous than the records, sorry, the statements you gave to the Prosecutor in 1998. This document is dated 1st of December, 1992 and relates to events occurring in the preceding eight months and it's based upon information you gathered over some period.

utterances.speaker: SIMO ZARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What you've said there, about Nikolic endorsing -- Nikolic and the 17th Tactical Group command endorsing this group, five or six days after they arrived and that, of course, is before the takeover -- is quite consistent with what you said in your statements about Nikolic having some responsibility for the takeover, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: SIMO ZARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: There is a certain connection, but you must allow me to give you my opinion in relation to this. It's very important when you read this text in B/C/S what is inside the quotation marks and it's very important how the information dealt with a certain problem. I have precisely, in this part of paragraph 2 that you are referring to, said that it is not contested that initially this group, the command of the 17th Tactical Group, was treated by the Commander Nikolic as a gang of gangsters and mercenaries. What I quoted was exactly what the commander had said, but it is also true that few days later, after Commander Nikolic received the information that this was a special unit, that it was linked to the authorities in some structures in Yugoslavia, then as far as I was concerned, at the time when this information was written, it was not to be denied that I should put this inside this information because if he was claiming that this team was a special unit and that he had even seen some IDs while we had found out in the meantime where they had come from and where they had trained, and I had already had the information through which structure they have arrived here, then of course, I think it's logical that such a critical assessment was given in this document. That's how I see this.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: But that's not what I'm asking you, Mr. Zaric, with respect. I'm asking you about your statement there, which -- the document you drafted and which everyone who has come to court that you've brought to court has testified was true and correct, and they signed it after a discussion, and they agreed with its contents, I'm asking you about the comment there, or your words, "But after only five or six days, they endorsed it." That is Nikolic and the 17th Tactical Group command, before the takeover, endorsed these paramilitaries. Now, that only suggests that they were acting with the JNA, if they were endorsed by the 17th Tactical Group command, doesn't it? I mean there is no other explanation you can give for what you've written there, is there?

utterances.speaker: SIMO ZARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. The only thing here is the fact that the commander had said that this group had a legitimate character on the basis of his interview with them, and that's why it's -- this assessment is between the quotation marks, that this has been verified and interpreted as, and then there are quotation marks as a legal, elite unit of Serb specials. That's what the commander had said that he had accepted as a fact because that's what he had been told. And what's very important afterwards, to be known, is that after these words, it says, "Whose arrival has been legalised through official organs of authority and army, not only on the level of the Samac municipality but also on the highest level in Serbia and Yugoslavia." And when this part was said, that's what I meant this to say, including people working on this information. If the commander of the 17th Corps [Realtime transcript read in error "Tactical Group"] Mr. Savo Jankovic, after the information that the group arrived, had said, "don't touch them, the army has nothing to do with that," if this information Savo Jankovic received from somebody from the army of Serbia, Yugoslavia, then I thought that the army had allowed this team, this group, to act as a special police unit. That's my explanation.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Small correction. When referring to Mr. Savo Jankovic, here on page 69, line 8, and 9, if the commander of the 17th Corps, Mr. Savo Jankovic is how it should be read, here is says, "If the commander of the 17th Tactical Group, Mr. Savo Jankovic." He was the commander of the 17th Corps.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes, it's obvious that that was a mistake.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: But this is of course -- this endorsement which you have referred to there only five or six days after their arrival, that is before the takeover, you're saying in this document that Nikolic and the command of the 17th Tactical Group were endorsing a group of paramilitaries, formerly called paramilitaries but then a legal elite of Serbian commandos, days after Serbian paramilitaries had taken over Zvornik, Bijeljina, Bosanski Brod and committed atrocities. That's what you're saying, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: SIMO ZARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. That's what you're saying. I'm not saying that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, but it goes further, Mr. Zaric, and that is when you were interviewed --

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: I apologise. This is maybe my understanding but --

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Is this an objection?

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Yes, actually it is an objection.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: I'll sit down.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: When quoting Mr. Zaric this you keep saying that was all before the takeover and now I was looking at all this, and it was not in dispute that the paramilitaries arrived on 11th. So six to seven days later --

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: I really object. You stop this. You stop this now.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: All right, this is my objection.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Mr. Re, don't be agitated. The document is clear. It says five or six days.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: That's right, the witness can answer it. Mr. Lazarevic cannot keep interjecting and cluing the witness, pointing out things. The witness has in front of him, it's his document, he can explain anything and he hasn't contradicted what I've said. If Mr. Lazarevic wishes to do so, he does it in closing submissions or re-examination. If I say something -- if I put a proposition to the witness, the witness can answer it, unless there is something objectionable about the question or the form. This happens all the time.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: I have no problem. I've left this question once, I left the question twice. The third time I reacted is because I have a belief that you are trying to confuse my client with these questions and this is what it is.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Mr. Lazarevic, the Trial Chamber doesn't think so, because Mr. Simo Zaric is discussing things within his knowledge, and matters which he has given -- already given evidence on. So let's have some order so that the Prosecution can continue cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: I do apologise to my learned friend and to the Trial Chamber, just a maybe it might be of certain importance to clarify transcript. Page 70, line between 9 and 12, I think the portion of question and answer should be split just for the record. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Which question and answer?

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: The first portion when my learned friend Mr. Re said, "I'll sit down," during the objection of my learned friend Lazarevic and then Mr. Lazarevic starts to speak.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: M'hm.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: So we have only one sentence between line 9 and 12, which is unclear part of transcript.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: I don't think it matters a lot. Let's proceed.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Zaric, you take it further about Mr. Nikolic having command of the paramilitary units. In your record of interview or your statement on the 1st of April, that's P140 ter, at page 73, do you have that one there, P140 ter at page 73?

utterances.speaker: SIMO ZARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, no, that's not this part.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Lazarevic was just motioning to me it was actually page 73. I was reading the English on page 73. I apologise but the question, the question is on page 73, the question "Nancy." The difficulty is they're both mixed in the same paragraph in this version. "Nancy: Okay, let me just ask a few questions to clarify some things. Did you ever learn anything about Crni and his background to understand why he was getting all the special attention and treatment?" You see that question there?

utterances.speaker: SIMO ZARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, no, no. It has not been found. We can't find that. I mean, the usher didn't tell me -- didn't give me this part. I don't know where to find it. I don't know which document --

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Perhaps I can assist.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: P140 ter.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I have a page in front of me, page 73, but now you'll have to remind me.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Middle of the page, don't turn the page.

utterances.speaker: SIMO ZARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Very well.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Nancy -- the paragraph is mixed English and B/C/S the first half is English the second half is B/C/S. Okay. Says Nancy, "Let me just ask you" --

utterances.speaker: SIMO ZARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Can you tell me -- yes, yes, "Only a few questions in order to clarify," yes, I found this part.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. Now, your answer about why Crni was singled out to be so important was, "I knew very little about him. All these people who came from elsewhere, they all just had nicknames and it was like a month and then when they said that he became brigade commander then he realised his name was -- that his name was Dragan Djurdjevic. Up until then he only knew he was Crni. He was always very, very close to Mr. Stevan Todorovic and the Serbian police. This is the point I wish to direct your attention to. At some point he was also made commander of the battalion and at some point, his superior was also Nikolic for a very short time before he left for Yugoslavia." Now, what -- you've read that and I've read it correctly to you, haven't I?

utterances.speaker: SIMO ZARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes, you have read it well.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What you've said there again is a reference to Nikolic having command at some point over the paramilitary, Crni. There is no other interpretation, I suggest, to what is said there, that Nikolic was his commander or superior at some point, is there?

utterances.speaker: SIMO ZARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: At that time, when I was giving this answer, Mrs. Nancy wasn't interested in elaborating on this as you're interested but when I linked Mr. Nikolic to Mr. Dragan Djurdjevic, also known as Crni, the only thing I meant was that in that part where he was a member of a special unit in a special battalion, in certain situations he was subordinate to Nikolic, if the Special Battalion was tasked with certain operations and there has been testimony to this effect here, and regarding this category of this relationship, that's what I meant. Not in a sense that Commander Nikolic was exclusively superior to Crni but only certain operations that the Special Battalion was carrying out, with the public security station. I don't know what they were attached to to start with.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I don't need Mr. Usher to stand there any more. If you just leave those there? Thank you. The -- did you take part yourself in any of these special operations in which the paramilitary units were subordinated to Colonel Nikolic?

utterances.speaker: SIMO ZARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I personally did not participate in that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: But in preparing the 13 signatories, that is P127 and spending all the time you did in researching the information for this very important document, you became aware and included in this report that, "The Special Battalion" - I'm just quoting from it which you can see in front of you there in the third paragraph - "played an indisputably positive role in the liberation of Samac as part of the Special Battalion in fighting in Vidovica, Kornice, Garevac, Kladari in the liberation of the corridor to Brcko and in other operations." That's the information you had when you prepared your report that these paramilitaries had worked with the JNA on those special operations, wasn't it?

utterances.speaker: SIMO ZARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This conclusion can be drawn, but I only wish to say, and I'm not trying to evade what it says here, but I have to say that I personally put a lot of effort into having the information adopted within the context in which I believed it should be used so that all the qualifications used in this document doesn't mean that it was Simo Zaric's desire that that's the qualification that should be used. However, I stood behind the assessment because it was far less important to me than the content of the rest of the information.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Zaric, I don't quite understand your answer. I've just simply asking you this was the information you had, namely that the paramilitaries, as part of the Special Battalion, had taken part in operations in those places I just named, with JNA troops. That was your information, wasn't it, and that's why you put it in this report?

utterances.speaker: SIMO ZARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Some people insisted that it should be included in the information and I was not in a position to change this. I didn't really want them mentioned, especially in any kind of positive context, but when this information was drawn up, and debated, there were people who insisted on this. They insisted that the liberation of Samac and the part of the corridor which was under attack from Brcko, Modrica, around Vidovica and so on where these special purpose units took part in the fighting, that they should be given this sort of recognition, which is why this sentence was included in the information. If you were to ask me whether I agreed that this should be in the information, I was not trying to praise this team, although I would like to tell Their Honours that out of the 20 or so specials that arrived, six of them were killed in our area, which is almost 20 per cent of their number, which arrived in this area, and so the people in the command wanted to recognise the fact that people had died for the struggle and that they had some sort of patriotic feelings because not all the specials were bandits like Lugar and others who committed crimes. I wouldn't agree that each and every one of them who arrived bore this characteristic.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: That's not what I'm asking you. Please concentrate. What I'm asking you is about the fact that they participated, I'm not interested whether it was positive or who insisted it go in there, your information was that these specials, Lugar, Crni, Debeli, them and their men, had participated in those operations, wasn't it?

utterances.speaker: SIMO ZARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. And they were then resubordinated to the command of the 17th Tactical Group, as far as I was able to learn later on. Only in these operations were they resubordinated to the command of the 17th Tactical Group. After that, they regained their former status.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Are you able to say how many operations these men were used in, subordinated to Nikolic?

utterances.speaker: SIMO ZARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know the exact number. I wasn't a commander of the 17th Tactical Group.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, I think you were saying a moment ago it was others who insisted that the information be put in the report. Is that right? Is that the sense of what you were saying that it was others not you who wanted that information in the report? I don't want a long answer but is that the gist of what you were saying?

utterances.speaker: SIMO ZARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Others insisted that they be ascribed a great merit for the liberation of Samac and I personally did not agree with this. As to their participation in certain operations, as a resubordinated unit, I think that the commander of the 17th Tactical Group was in charge of that, and he was the only one who was in charge of it.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You still have your book there in front of you?

utterances.speaker: SIMO ZARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: If you turn to I think it's about page 297 to 298, it's just near the photo caption at page 298, the few paragraphs above the photo caption?

utterances.speaker: SIMO ZARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Tell me how the paragraph begins and I'll try to find my way.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: It's the fourth paragraph after 2, so it's on page 298. It starts, "In brief, we analysed certain events and phenomena which demoralised soldiers and weakened the unit's combat efficiency and readiness, as we say in military terminology."

utterances.speaker: SIMO ZARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't find these exact words but does it mean anything to you if I start reading, "In brief, we carried out an analysis of certain events and phenomena"? Am I near the place where you want me to read?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: That's the paragraph. It's that one and the next one. Just read those two to yourself, please.

utterances.speaker: SIMO ZARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I've read it.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You see the paragraph there, after you've referred to their arrival and the way they were treated as a "quite legitimate Serb elite unit of specially trained men," you go on to say "but we did not begrudge them the recognition they deserved. Their significant role in the Defence of Samac, in the fighting at Vidovica, Kornice, Garevac, Kladari, and in the opening of the corridor. We also talked about the contribution of 'local special units' but things that were inexcusable in the behaviour of the volunteers, plunder, robbery, crime, the crime at Crkvina, were called by their real names and attributed to key persons in positions of responsibility." Now, what you've said in that book there is in relation to the report, isn't it, just yes or no? That's yes? You're nodding, yes?

utterances.speaker: SIMO ZARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You see, what you've said there is we did not begrudge them the recognition they deserved, their significant role in defence of Samac and the fighting at Vidovica, et cetera. You haven't said there, "I reluctantly included a reference to these people, I didn't want to do it, other people insisted on it, I thought their bad outweighed their good." You haven't said that in your book. What you have said is you're not begrudging them the recognition they deserve.

utterances.speaker: SIMO ZARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: There was no need for me to justify myself in the way you want me to. I tried to reproduce in the most honest way what the information contained, and out of respect for the people who signed this information, at the end I also mentioned the names of all the people who signed this information. This is on page 300. Therefore, at that moment, I was dealing with what the information says, not what Simo Zaric himself thought, and it was proper on my part to say, "We did not pass over what had to be conceded to them, an important role in the defence of Samac, in battles at Vidovica, Kornice, Garevac, Kladari and in establishing the corridor." I was simply saying what was in the information in paragraph 2. In the book I didn't want to make excuses for myself saying this was not my opinion, but the opinion of 13 signatories. I tried to show the public what the purpose of the information was, and as the author of the book, what did the author want to say? Simo Zaric only wanted to transmit in an authentic manner what was contained in the information, not passing over anything.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You also talked about the paramilitaries in an interview you gave to Omri on the 16th of November, 1996. That's Omri, the Croatian, sorry, the Czech media, you gave two interviews to Omri, one was in the presence of Mr. Pisarevic on the 12th of November, and the second was in your own office which was next to your food store in Bosanski Samac on the 16th of November, 1996.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Yes, and I object of using these documents in the course of cross-examination of Mr. Zaric. First of all, just to assure the Trial Chamber we have received them and they have been disclosed to us. But I want this document to have the same treatment as were interviews of Mr. Miroslav Tadic to the investigators of the Prosecution before he actually received his indictment. In November, 1996, Mr. Zaric hasn't received his indictment yet. He was not aware of the content of the indictment. It seems from what we received from the Prosecution, that it was done for ICTY, as it states here, that it was done for some purposes of the ICTY by some persons. Frankly, I don't know what this version means OMRI Sarajevo, what this is, but obviously if we take a look at one of these documents, it says that, and I'm quoting right now, that a lawyer of Mr. Zaric, meaning, of course, Mr. Pisarevic, "who then ended the talk and asking us to hand -- to be handed over our report or article for final approval before publishing. Such an approval was never given." So at the moment, when certain persons and one of them was obviously a qualified in some investigations, interviewed Mr. Simo Zaric, he was not aware of the full content of the indictment. He was not aware even of the names of all the crimes he was charged for. He was not informed on his rights that this can be used against him, and finally, his attorney, who was present at the moment, asked for final approval for publishing this documents. And such an approval was never given. And just one thing that I would like to add, here it says exclusively for Bill Stuebner, I don't know who this gentleman is, and ICTY only. It was obviously done for ICTY. So I would like to ask for dismissal --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: I don't understand the part where you are saying it was obviously done for ICTY only. What are you saying?

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Neither do I, Your Honour, because this is the document that we received as an interview of Mr. Zaric given to some persons which I never found out who these persons belonged to, and here, on these documents, it says, "Exclusively for Bill Stuebner and ICTY only." That -- suggesting that this interview or document or whatever it is, was done for ICTY.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: M'hm.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: So according to the ruling of this Trial Chamber in relation to the interviews that Mr. Tadic gave to the investigators of the OTP, and also the Prosecution asked for admission of these interviews and the ruling of the Trial Chamber was that it won't be tendered into evidence, it won't be used against Mr. Tadic because he was not aware of all the indictments that were against him, the contents of the indictment, or his rights and particularly that this might be used against him.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Your Honour?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Lukic?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I wish to say something on behalf of the Defence of my client, because the content in these papers, not to say documents, also refer to my Defence so I would like to put forward the standpoint of the Defence of Mr. Tadic in connection with the documents that the Prosecution is now using. I don't know whether they wish to tender them into evidence. I will only say very briefly that what it says in this so-called interview, the questions in it are directly related to the counts in the indictment, and I think that here, the right to defence has been violated in an even more flagrant manner than in the case of Mr. Tadic, because questions directly related to the counts, the questions are directly related to the counts, and Mr. Zaric at the time did not even have the first indictment which was sent to him by fax and especially not the second one, which includes persecution. In Rule 95, it says that evidence collected in -- by methods that cast serious doubt on their reliability, on its reliability or if its admission is antithetical to and would seriously damage the integrity of the proceedings, it shall not be admissible so I think that the Prosecution should tell us how they came by these documents and why the accused is being shown this interview, which he gave while he was being misled or when he was in error, didn't understand what was going on, so I think that it is very clear, I think that Rule 89 authorises the Trial Chamber not to permit the integrity of the proceedings to be brought into question so I think we should now find out how this interview was made and I think that according to 89(D), the Chamber may exclude this evidence. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Re?

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: I wouldn't suggest my learned friends are deliberately misleading the Trial Chamber but we are apparently looking at completely different documents, if those are the submissions from Mr. Lukic and Mr. Lazarevic. They are two documents we have which the Defence has too. They are transcripts of interviews between two journalists from OMRI which is called the Open Media Research Institute. It is a Balkan publishing institute which used to publish a daily digest on events in the Balkans. After the indictments were published and no one had turned themselves in to the Tribunal, the journalists, namely -- whose names are clearly in the front of the -- Mr. Pisarevic knows because he was there, Mr. Jan-- I'm not sure if it's Jan, a woman, or Jan, a man, Jan or Jan Urban and Yvonne Badal, B-a-d-a-l, interviewed Mr. Zaric in Bosanski Samac. They went looking for people who had been indicted. They were trying to prove how easy it was to find people who had been indicted in the Balkans and they even wrote a story about it in which they said since October 29, when the Boston Globe found four indicted war criminals working in the Prijedor or Omarska Police Station, more evidence has surfaced suggesting that not only does the Republika Srpska government openly protect war criminals but also that it is IFOR's deliberate policy for now not to arrest them. They then refer to going to saying two international police took photos and video footage of the workplace and houses of at least two indicted war criminals, I don't mean that -- presumption of innocence, of course. I'm just reading from the document, Simo Zaric and Miroslav Tadic. Zaric himself told OMRI, "I went through IFOR checkpoints hundreds of times." It's an interview between two journalists of a Czech-based publishing outfit, as I understand it, a non-profit one. The first one occurred on the 12th of November, 1996, place: Office of his lawyer in Bosanski Samac, that is Mr. Pisarevic. Present: Jan or Jan Urban, Yvonne Badal, lawyer Borislav X named to be confirmed, they then confirmed it, Simo Zaric and a person called NN, in brackets, RS army, personal friend of Zaric. They then reinterviewed Mr. Zaric four days later, in his own office place, Zaric's private office beside his food store in Bosanski Samac, date November the 16th, 1996, present, Jan Urban, Yvonne Badal, Simo Zaric and NN. The only person missing at that time was Mr. Pisarevic. And the reasons are there. They wanted to speak to Mr. Zaric in the absence of his lawyer, for reasons which are unnecessary to go into. And they asked him questions about the indictment and about what had happened in Bosanski Samac during the war. And his view of the indictments against the other people, and I wasn't intending to go anywhere near that, and they asked him about certain events that occurred in Bosanski Samac. Now, at some point, the interviewers decided to do their public duty, as they probably thought it was, seeing that no one had turned themselves in and here we have Mr. Zaric in the presence of his lawyer, being interviewed about this very matter, about the fact that he is going through IFOR checkpoints all the time, and they faxed these two interviews to the ICTY and that is why it has written on the top, "Exclusively for Bill Stuebner and ICTY only." It said, "Upon Bill's request and in order not to complicate any further meetings between ICTY and lawyer Pisarevic on Croatian territory, we will refrain from mentioning ICTY-lawyer contacts in our articles." It has nothing at all to do with the ICTY and in fact it has in large letters, your typical embargo, media embargo, "Not for public use before November 19," which is the OMRI publishing date. It is simply an interview between Mr. Zaric and two journalists which he freely gave in the same way that he wrote a book after his indictment and in his book spoke to Croatian or Serbian journalists from Croatian media, and whether or not Mr. Pisarevic checked it or thought that he had some right of embargo over its contents before it was published is irrelevant. And the first one, the second one, clearly said at the bottom, we explained that we were going to do a shorter piece in OMRI's WWW and a longer one in either the New York Times or the Washington Post. He, Mr. Zaric, thought for quite sometime and asked us not to. So as a result, they didn't publish it, but they transmitted the record of interview or the record of the interview to the ICTY. I wish to ask Mr. Zaric some questions on these long-disclosed documents as to some of the things he said to these two journalists. Now --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes, but from what you have said, Mr. Zaric had said that they shouldn't publish the interview.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: In the New York Times or the Washington Post.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Is that exactly what he said or was it publishing generally or in particular to those two and the implication would be that he wouldn't mind it published to anybody else other than those two newspapers? Is that clear.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: That's not what it says. It says, "We explained we were going to do a shorter piece in OMRI's WWW" - obviously their Internet site - "and a longer one in either the New York Times and Washington Post he thought for quite sometime and then asked us not to." That refers to -- they do different things, daily reports and opinion pieces they published. What they did publish was a piece in the -- it's called an analytical brief, in which they explained how they managed to find him. In my submission, I mean it has nothing to do with the ICTY at all. It's in the nature of an explanation Mr. Zaric has given of events at the time when questioned, when aware that he had been indicted and the interviewers refer to the indictment and - the first one of course - in the presence of his lawyer who has been advising him for many, many years. It's not an investigative statement. It has no analogy at all to the Tadic record of interview which was the ICTY interviewing Mr. Tadic after he telephoned the ICTY offering to talk to them. We understand that the indictment wasn't properly faxed through and Your Honours's judgement there. This is an entirely different document, category. It's something that someone has said to the media and it gets published. It's like a the book. It's like the Croatian one that Mr. Pisarevic was objecting to in his book which his book says he objected to. It's just a normal statement which someone has made which may or may not be --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Because the background from what you've explained, it was after the indictment was published and then these reporters or journalists went looking for the indictees. And then they found them and started talking to them and after that they faxed the interview, one of the places was to the ICTY.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: That's right. It's not improperly or illegally obtained.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: But he wasn't told that they would fax it to the ICTY. Like he was asked about publication on the other -- in the other aspect where he said no.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Is there any difference in my submission between talking to journalists and not expecting journalists to publish something on the Internet or in the New York Times?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Because this was not an ordinary interview. These people had the indictment and from what you've said, they were looking for the indictees.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: That's right and they had Mr. Pisarevic as well. They conducted the interview, the first one, in the presence of his lawyer. And in fact, the first is a transcript of the lawyer, Mr. Pisarevic, starting off by saying, "Let me begin with the more general picture, we are in contact with the ICTY," et cetera, et cetera. And there is a lot of objections by Mr. Pisarevic in this particular document. It's in the presence of his lawyer who is aware of the indictment.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WILLIAMS
utterances.text: I just have one small question. You were saying that Mr. Zaric refused to have publication of a smaller piece. I think those were the words you used a smaller piece in the New York Times and the Washington Post. Do I infer from that correctly that there was another piece that was actually published based on these same interviews?

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: The only thing I can find in my own search on the Internet of the OMRI site was an article analytical brief number 481. It didn't have a date on it in which they referred to speaking to Mr. Zaric. I don't intend to interpret it. I only say what it actually says there. But there is certainly nothing of that nature in the first interview which was conducted in Mr. Pisarevic who I think has a conflict of interest if he wishes to -- because he's a witness to these matters. There is certainly nothing in the second or first record of interview, first interview with the journalists in relation to non-publication.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: I believe that this is not quite correct. I apologise. I will give the floor but because it is in English.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Excuse me, I didn't realise that we have run over our time because of the support we asked for from the interpreters and -- Mr. Pisarevic, you wanted to make submissions?

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, but I can do it after the break.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Let's take our break.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Your Honour, could we have five minutes more our break?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: I think eight minutes more because that's what we've gone over.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Pisarevic?

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Your Honours, before Mr. Pisarevic speaks, could I just say, in case there is any misunderstanding, first of all the Prosecution doesn't intend to tender those documents, all we would be doing would be asking Mr. Zaric if this is what he said and if it's true. That's normal. We don't have an audio of those documents, or any way of independently verifying the truth except for Mr. Pisarevic who is standing over there which leads me to my second point, that in the Prosecution he's submission, Mr. Pisarevic, I reluctantly say this, has a conflict of interest in making submissions on this point for this reason, that if Your Honours were to admit testimony in relation to the -- or allow cross-examination, he was a witness to what was said and if his client were to deny it, he could be a witness in the proceedings so in my submission, he has a potential conflict, if not an actual one, in intervening in the proceedings, which is why we have co-counsel.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: At the beginning, in your own submission, you did say that the interview was in the presence of his lawyer, so I'm expecting that he's making whatever submission is going to make, it's as to what the occasion was. Not what was said, because we haven't yet jumped to the stage whether or not what was said can be cited in this Trial Chamber.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Of course I understand that but the difficulty is the Prosecution perceives it is that Mr. Pisarevic could be a witness to what was said and in the interests of perception of no conflict, it would be preferable if his co-counsel were to deal with this matter, if necessary, on instructions from Mr. Pisarevic. Because otherwise, Mr. Pisarevic could be making submissions on it and something could arise later depending upon Your Honour's decision. That's all.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: I will first find out what Mr. Pisarevic wants to deal with.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honours. I am not going to go into the contents of the interview. I just want to say the following: That is that this interview, which is reportedly as it says here, they were -- these interviews were made up -- were made but we never saw them. When these gentlemen came, they did not come with a person unknown, as it says here, NN, friend of Simo Zaric, officer of Republika Srpska, but it was the owner of Alternativa Publishing Company from Doboj by the last name of Stankovic so it was not an officer of the Republika Srpska who was present. That was the first thing.
